Not infrequently, they approach their work as a way to earn something now so they can eventually make an "honest" living in the future; what escapes them is that there is nothing dishonest about refusing to hand over protection money, even when we call it taxes—it is still a coerced payment made under the threat of violence. Having spread this perspective for nearly twenty years, I have had countless opportunities to witness the relief of someone who considered themselves a bad person, yet upon adopting an anarchist view of the world realized they are doing nothing morally wrong, even though society had convinced them otherwise since childhood; and the theories of the Austrian School of economics in turn show them that their illegal activity does not diminish anyone's well-being either—quite the opposite.

I consider participation in the gray economy one of the keys to freedom. Every crown we surrender to public coffers can be used to curtail our liberties; yet that is far from all—with every service provided outside the reach of state power, we demonstrate in practice that we do not need a central authority to run our lives, because we are capable of doing it far better ourselves. Personally, I try to avoid making payments to the state, as well as taking anything from it so as not to become dependent on it; I cannot fully achieve either—I cannot completely avoid taxation (especially indirect taxes), nor can I avoid using services in state-monopolized sectors (for example, I use roads). Still, I try to minimize both: I don't pay taxes I don't have to, and above all, I do not work for the state and have never in my life taken any money from it, even though I could have. There are libertarians who, on the contrary, draw as much from the state as possible in order to weaken it. While I understand their arguments, I do not identify with that approach for two reasons: first, for as long as I can remember, I have felt a strong emotional aversion to accepting coercively extracted money (if I were to do it myself, I would not feel right about it, even though it does not trigger those emotions in me when others do it); above all, however, I want to be as independent of central power as possible (which is also why I have been saving for retirement my entire life, so that I won't have to take state money even in my old age).

Often, I can not only ignore public authority, but also peacefully do my part to paralyze it by tying up the resources it uses to target me whenever I happen to have the capacity for it. One example is a roadside (or any other) inspection that the state sends my way, even when I am harming no one (and even when everything is in order according to the law itself). I can hinder and slow down the course of such an inspection (sometimes quite effectively, if I know the relevant legislation), which on the one hand prevents them from bothering someone else at the same time, and above all means I do not bow before the enforcers of state power. They are accustomed to a submissive attitude from those they inspect, as a result of which they generally take more liberties; the more often they encounter resistance (even within the bounds of complete politeness), the less they dare—and moreover, their job becomes less attractive to individuals eager to bully others from a position of power. The art of dealing with state officials as equals (I am not talking about rudeness or looking down on them) also expands the horizons of our (primarily inner) freedom.

The goal of anarcho-agorism is to build parallel structures of sufficient relevance and strength that, while the state might not necessarily vanish as an organization, it would no longer be able to enforce its monopoly on violence against them; its legislation would thus become irrelevant to a portion of society. Anarcho-agorists would then no longer mind that statists choose to keep living under the laws of their rulers; their agoras would follow their own order, independent of any government. Something like this likely presupposes an armed populace willing to defend itself against violence; however, that does not mean the process cannot unfold peacefully—the establishment may choose not to attack and risk a bloody civil war if the anticipated resistance is too great. Nothing of the sort is imaginable today, yet if a non-negligible share of society lives in accordance with anarcho-agorist principles, the state will naturally begin to shrink and lose the strength to exercise its power. We are certainly nowhere near that point today; nevertheless, we can already create islands of freedom where the power of external authorities reaches only to a limited extent.

How does anarcho-agorism relate to anarcho-capitalism? I believe both schools of thought share the same goal—namely, a free, free-market society—yet they differ in their approach to reaching that goal. Whereas anarcho-agorists reject the political path, anarcho-capitalists neither reject it nor require it; this means an anarcho-capitalist can also be an anarcho-agorist (for instance, I am both), but does not have to be. There are also anarcho-agorists who do not consider themselves anarcho-capitalists, because to them "capitalism" evokes corporate fascism rather than a free market. Personally, I consider anarcho-agorism to be a "pure" version of anarcho-capitalism, in the sense that its (non-political) means do not contradict its (non-political) end.

Before we turn to disobedience in the next chapter, I would like to warn against certain counterproductive steps on the road to freedom. Please, let us not restrict the freedom of people we believe are doing something wrong; if they want to be led by someone and form (voluntary) hierarchies, let us not stand in their way (after all, anyone who needs leadership will eventually find it anyway), even if it may seem dangerous to us—let us not launch preemptive strikes. In my view, the better path is to engage in dialogue, especially as long as no one is (physically) attacking. Meet words with words, and a sword (at most) with a sword. And even words can be used peacefully (albeit clearly and unwaveringly); berating people as enemies of freedom typically will not turn them into its friends.

name: 16. Disobedience
text:
I consider disobedience to be an essential personal prerequisite for anyone seeking to embark on the anarcho-agorist path. I do not mean that if (perhaps due to our upbringing) we gravitate toward obedience, we cannot be anarcho-agorists; however, I consider it important to become conscious of our (dis)obedience and work with it. Since we live in a state-managed society—and most people accept the state at least as a necessity, or even deify it to some degree—this puts varying degrees of social pressure on anarchists; obedient or proud citizens may see us as a danger and a threat to their way of life. We can regularly observe this most starkly during election periods, when non-voters often provoke greater hostility among voters than supporters of rival political camps; they want us to conform—and it is precisely our disobedience that allows us to resist going with the crowd and to live in accordance with our values. Yet what actually is (dis)obedience?

Developmental psychologist Lawrence Kohlberg defined six stages of moral development: fear of punishment; desire for reward; need for relationships (typically manifesting as an effort to please others); blind obedience to laws (regardless of their content); acceptance of the social contract (which stands above laws, meaning laws must be changed or interpreted for the benefit of society); and finally, living according to one's own ethical values and rules (regardless of any legislation). I agree with his conclusions, though I believe they are (at least in the early stages) relevant primarily in an environment where punishments or rewards serve as the basic tools of upbringing aimed at making a child obedient; and obedience to parents or teachers easily turns into blind obedience to laws. After all, Kohlberg himself notes that only 15% of people over the age of 25 reach the fifth stage, while he describes the sixth as largely "potential," because even those who reason at that level typically cannot consistently align their opinions (let alone their actions) with it.

For the purposes of anarcho-agorism, I have outlined four layers of (dis)obedience. The first layer is defined by the view that we ought to follow legislation; this does not mean people holding this belief can never break laws (even intentionally), only that they generally do not consider it right. The second layer can be summed up by the phrase: "If you don't like a law, change it." We hear this refrain frequently, especially from advocates of democracy; their means of changing the world lie in politics or civic activism. What leads to the third layer is the realization that lawmakers are only human and their knowledge of our lives is necessarily very limited, so they can hardly design better rules for us than we can for ourselves. The logical way out is then conscious disobedience toward legislation that conflicts with what we consider right; even so, we may sometimes choose to obey a bad law rather than face the consequences (just as individuals in the first layer may violate legal norms)—the layers of (dis)obedience describe a person's internal mindset rather than their conduct in every single situation. Yet when we break a law, we may help ourselves, while the bad legislation itself remains in society. What can we do about that? The answer lies in the fourth layer: we can help others break laws too, show them ways, inspire them, and share the necessary knowledge and skills. Doing so is often illegal in itself, and therefore risky; however, it can (if necessary) be carried out more or less covertly (we will say more about this in the Practice and Participation chapters).

Why do I regard trying to change laws as a "lower" layer of (dis)obedience than breaking them? First, it is a matter of efficiency—changing legislation requires expending an enormous amount of energy that can be used far more productively not only in finding ways to break or circumvent it, but even in sharing that knowledge (disobedience scales well in an environment where information spreads easily, which today's society provides very well). Above all, however, I consider it more ethical—I would rather violate state law than compromise my own moral integrity in trying to change it (two chapters ago I explained why I see politics as a very dirty game); nor do I wish to lend legislation an appearance of legitimacy by seriously engaging in making it, when instead I can diminish its legitimacy in the eyes of others through disrespect for it and thereby foster an environment where, rather than formal norms, we care about not infringing on anyone's freedom, property, and the like. I view obedience as one of the most dangerous viruses of our civilization—and breaking laws is one of the key ingredients of the antivirus.

Here I will take the liberty of recalling Howard Zinn's quote once again: "Civil disobedience is not our problem. Our problem is civil obedience. Our problem is that people all over the world obeyed the orders of leaders; and because of that obedience, millions of people were killed." A massive error in assessing the harmfulness of obedience lies in considering its effects only in the good times of relatively peaceful societies, where it typically results in the "mere" imprisonment of individuals who have harmed no one (and who moreover make up only a fraction of a percent of the entire population). Once we also take into account its consequences in wartime and under totalitarian regimes (which could never even come into existence without obedience), disobeying laws ceases to look like such a dangerous alternative.

However, I consider it truly vital not to confuse disobedience with self-serving defiance or blind rebellion; that may help us at some stage along the life journey from obedience to disobedience, yet ultimately it is just obedience in "disguise" once again. If we automatically start doing the opposite of whatever someone orders us to do, that person is still controlling our life—only in the opposite direction from what they intend. If, however, we want to live on our own terms and for ourselves, defiance against someone or something is not the answer. I know people who say they don't trust the government (fair enough, neither do I), yet in practice this means they tend to believe the opposite of everything the government says; that approach does not help much in the search for truth. When COVID first began and I knew practically nothing about it, I put on a mask—voluntarily, even before any government mandate—and since wearing it didn't bother me, I stuck with it; for this I caught sharp criticism from some fellow anarchists accusing me of being a sheep blindly following politicians' orders. Yet taking off the mask solely because it had become mandatory would not have been disobedience, but blind defiance or caving in to peer pressure. I wore it (obviously not inside a car, as the legislation also required at the time) until it stopped making sense to me—which was somewhat earlier than the state allowed, yet long after not wearing a mask had become the badge of rebellion some expected of me.

Although I have no trouble refusing to go with the crowd or living the way I want and need, I do not believe I will ever reach a point where I am permanently and perfectly disobedient—that is, completely myself. I realize I fall into the trap of blind defiance more easily than into direct obedience, and I try to work with that so that with every step toward my true self I uncover further (albeit ever subtler) traces of obedience. Every year my son and I go to a Formula 1 Grand Prix, where the host country's national anthem always plays before the race, causing hundreds of thousands of people to stand up at once while I remain seated because I do not want to show reverence to any state (usually earning only a few disapproving looks). Just this year, however, I happened to be packing up my things and was about to stand up at the exact moment the anthem started—my first automatic reaction was to deliberately stay seated; only a few moments later did I realize I didn't actually want to rebel, but simply to sit or stand according to my own needs. Not that sitting or standing mattered at all in that instance; I see it, however, as a good illustration of something inside me that can of course manifest itself in far more substantive matters. Surely everyone understands that disobedience does not mean doing something just because someone tells us to; yet neither is it rebelling without a cause—disobedience means being yourself.

The subtitle of this book is "Good people don't obey bad laws." Yet who are the good people? And which laws are the bad ones? What do I actually mean by that? As follows from the preceding chapters, I consider bad laws to be all laws that restrict someone's negative (property) rights—that is, (external) freedom; this includes, among other things, any legislation that guarantees anyone any positive rights (I explain this relationship in greater detail in the Crime chapter). This is, of course, merely my own view; someone else might label entirely different laws as bad. And what if someone who wants to murder people in violation of the law considers themselves a good person? Even that can happen—which does not mean I agree with it: the purpose of this book is not to justify any aggression against anyone, but on the contrary to appeal for respect toward everyone, even where the law demands the opposite. With that subtitle, I am trying to express my conviction that even though I realize that if people started following what they themselves consider right instead of existing legislation, it would bring plenty of problems, we would still prevent far greater suffering.

name: 17. Self-development
text:
In the previous chapter, I mentioned that disobedience means being yourself. Yet what does that mean? From early childhood, we are pushed to be good boys and girls, to make something of ourselves, to get somewhere in life (even though no one really knows what or where), to outperform siblings, classmates, or the children of our parents' neighbors and colleagues so that someone can be proud of us. Under the weight of these demands, we pile on layers of false identities—imaginary people who handle everything, never complain, have no struggles, and always figure things out. The more effectively we pull this off, the farther we drift from our true "self," which may happen to be sad or long for something incompatible with a given society's accepted image of a successful individual; so we sever contact with this inconvenient "self," burying it so deeply that we lose access to its needs. How, then, can we be disobedient? How can we be ourselves?

I consider it crucial to understand the process of how this happened in the first place. From a very young age, we are expected to obey teachers, parents, and also all sorts of social norms—everything that "is done" or "is not done"—behind which specific people's needs may be hidden, though often there aren't any at all. I once rode a bus where a very small child, whose feet could not even reach the floor yet, began kicking the seat in front of them; when the mother asked the child to stop, the child asked why. Her reaction surprised me: "Because you don't do that. Do you see anyone else kicking their seat?" I can hardly imagine a worse answer. Aside from appealing to an unspecified norm, rejecting difference, and demanding uniformity, it completely ignores any human needs—not even I could tell from that sentence what she actually cared about. Was it the comfort of the passenger in front? Keeping the seat clean? Did the child's movement bother her? Was she afraid the child might fall on the floor? Perhaps all of those together, or something else entirely; yet she did not try to convey any reason to the child, anyone's need—she demanded blind obedience and conformity. Just to prevent any misunderstanding, let me add that I am obviously not defending kicking seats; I am commenting strictly on the rationale given for why not to do it.

Society drills into us that wanting something for oneself is not as lofty and noble as defending the interests of others; people (including parents) therefore often hide their wishes behind something higher and more general. For instance, they won't tell "their" children that they are afraid others might judge them for the children's behavior, and instead appeal to common decency; they often deal with feeling threatened by another person's emotions by trying to regulate the child's outward expression; instead of speaking about their own need for peace and quiet, they might talk about what good children do or don't do; and they most commonly disguise their inability or unwillingness to let go of control as concern for safety, and so on. Children then adopt this way of communicating—and above all, of thinking—as their own, since they constantly learn by imitation, and subsequently hide their real needs behind general norms. Once they make this automatic enough, over time they grow so disconnected from their needs that they stop noticing them altogether—and eventually raise the next generation in the same spirit.

If we want to break this chain, we need to start getting to know ourselves. What do we truly want? What are our wishes, goals, desires, and dreams? And how do we distinguish them from the expectations of those around us? First, we need to pause and grant ourselves time—set aside work and daily tasks and attend only to what is inside us, how we feel, and what we are experiencing, striving for the utmost honesty and doing so repeatedly. How much time do we spend planning or choosing a vacation, a car, a job, or a house? And isn't being in touch with our "self" even more important? Different approaches suit different people: one prefers solitude in nature, another spends a few days on a darkness retreat, a third visits a therapist, coach, or shaman, and a fourth might turn to psychedelics (which can be effective, though also quite risky—especially for inexperienced and poorly informed users). All of these (and many other paths) often lead to the realization that we are living life according to someone else's expectations rather than doing what fulfills us.

Sometimes, along with seeing how we do not want to live, what we need immediately becomes clear as well; if we are too disconnected from our "self," however, only confusion may follow. What then? Step by step, explore our inner world, change different aspects of our life, and observe how that feels. Only one thing is certain—it will hurt, because for it to work and for us to learn, we have to leave our comfort zone (both during the discovery phase and when making life changes). It is not an easy path, yet it is definitely worth it; the reward lies not only in a happier existence, but also in self-knowledge and (inner) freedom, from which further fascinating and profound consequences follow.

Through self-development, we arrive at—among other things—the recognition, conviction, and above all genuine understanding and acceptance that we alone bear responsibility for our lives; we are the ones creating them. The creator's stance lies in realizing that whatever we carry within us is ultimately "ours," and if we want change, bringing it about likewise rests on us—we are the architects of our own happiness and unhappiness. The opposite of this attitude is the victim role. When we see ourselves as a victim, we search for culprits to blame for our misery—parents, politicians, the rich, the times we live in, the state, capitalism, genetics, a (former) partner, and the like. For example, someone addicted to alcohol, viewing things from the creator's perspective, understands that however they got into their condition, it is up to them how they deal (or don't deal) with their addiction; in the victim mindset, by contrast, that same person shifts attention away from themselves onto others—alcohol producers, unregulated advertising, an indifferent society, or drinking buddies. Each of us can look at the world through the lens of creator or victim; we are not aware of this choice in every moment, yet we can learn it (through persistent work on ourselves). The more time we spend as victims, the more susceptible we become to obedience—we believe someone else is responsible for our suffering, so all a would-be "leader" has to do is point out sufficiently believable culprits and offer a solution. Those "authors of evil" can be Jews, bourgeois, kulaks, or migrants, just as easily as Russians, Germans, Americans, or representatives of the state. Nor does it matter all that much whether or to what extent those in question actually harm us; what matters is whether someone (typically a politician) can convince us to focus on fighting them instead of focusing on our own lives and values. Of course, one cannot rule out the possibility that protecting and defending our own integrity might bring us into conflict with members of one of the groups above; what I consider absolutely crucial, however, is whether we do only what is necessary to protect ourselves, our loved ones (or other people), or whether we join a holy war in which we try to turn all our pain and anger against those we deem responsible for it (which we can easily rationalize as mere self-defense), thereby often becoming the very aggressors we oppose.

How do we become immune to false saviors exploiting us for their own interests? If we believe someone other than ourselves can be responsible for our suffering, or that someone other than ourselves can secure our happiness, we can be persuaded whom (and against whom) we ought to (blindly) follow in order to solve our problems. Conversely, the full realization that no such person exists (and cannot even exist in principle, because our life is solely and exclusively our responsibility) enables us to resist all such temptations, as in this context they do not even make sense. It follows that the more fiercely we yearn in "righteous anger" to punish, say, communists or Nazis for the atrocities committed in the name of their ideologies, the more easily we will succumb to the allure of some modern-day Stalin or Hitler. The principle remains the same—it is always about the urge to fight alongside or against someone rather than striving to live on one's own terms.

Just as obedience manifests both directly (by following) and indirectly (by defying at all costs), we can fall into the trap of refusing to take responsibility for our lives both as someone's followers and as leaders. The stronger someone's urge to lead people, impose order or justice on society, and build a better world for others, the more easily they succumb to the illusion that such things can be achieved "from above." Nor does it have to be the state; even anarchist "leaders of the revolution" cast themselves in the role of violent rulers (if only temporarily). In every case, it overlooks the principle that each person is responsible precisely for their own life—just as it makes no sense for someone else to be responsible for mine, it makes no more sense for me to be responsible for the lives of others.

Countless books, seminars, and all kinds of online content are devoted to self-development. In this chapter, I have tried to summarize only what is most relevant to disobedience and anarcho-agorism; unfortunately, this is merely the tip of the iceberg (in reality, self-development is a comprehensive path toward mastering fear, and thus toward inner freedom), and skimming only across its surface at that. I expect the following thoughts may have crossed many readers' minds while reading the last few paragraphs:

• But sometimes I really can become someone's victim! Am I supposed to pretend it didn't happen?

• In a perfect world, everyone would be the architect of their own happiness; in practice, no—some people are lucky, others unlucky.

• What if some group of people is genuinely hurting me? Am I just not supposed to defend myself, or what?

• I can't wait around for someone to attack me; I'll strike first!

• In order to live my life in peace, I logically first have to defeat those who interfere with it.

• When someone hurts people, they deserve a just punishment.

• In hard times and crises, people simply need a leader.

• This text is excusing aggressors and predators—it's blaming the victims! The more strongly someone identifies with these claims, the more I suspect that dedicating time to self-development could give them at least some intriguing food for thought. Where to begin? There are countless resources—an internet search engine or artificial intelligence will surely point the way; among foreign authors I can personally recommend Marshall Rosenberg (his Nonviolent Communication [NVC] changed my life), among Czech ones Pavel Moric, or my own podcast Zrzka a Matfyzák. Different things suit different people, and there is no single universally right method; still, I consider it more or less impossible to live inwardly free or effectively achieve external freedom without getting to know oneself (and conversely, ignorance of one's inner self often leads to disastrous or even fatal consequences—a freedom fighter can easily become an oppressor without even noticing it).

name: 18. Sharing
text:
SEK3 concluded The New Libertarian Manifesto with the cry: "Agora. Anarchy. Action!" While writing this book, slightly different words came to me (though with a similar meaning): "Freedom; self-direction; self-development; sharing." I trust I have sufficiently explained the meaning of the first three in earlier chapters; I would like to devote this one specifically to sharing. Why is it so important? And what do I actually mean by it? It encompasses both the voluntary transfer of material goods between people (whether in exchange for something, through lending, or through gift-giving just for the good feeling) and the spread of intangible goods, above all information. I believe that in the long run, all of this cumulatively leads to an increase in our degree of freedom—not necessarily every individual action, but taken together as a whole, more often than not—so that simply by interacting with one another in various ways, we end up moving toward freedom, which I find reassuring.

Let us start with material goods: voluntary exchange, lending, and gifts (free-market interactions do not necessarily have to be aimed at financial profit) make the division of labor possible, thereby raising the efficiency of human endeavor and thus the level of prosperity. Without the ability to access the fruits of others' labor, we would stand no better chance of survival than a naked castaway on a desert island. By far the best tool for allocating resources among strangers is money and the price system; it is only thanks to it that we can effectively transmit information (as well as incentives) dispersed throughout society, whose complexity no human brain can even grasp, let alone sensibly plan (which, fortunately, isn't even necessary). In smaller communities—agoras, families, tribes, and the like—it is possible to get by meaningfully without pricing. That (along with millions of years of evolution in small bands) leads some people to the mistaken belief that billions of individuals can organize themselves the same way, which at the current state of knowledge is not (and perhaps never will be) possible, even assuming the best intentions from everyone involved; without money and a price system, we cannot effectively communicate information about human needs or the scarcity of goods on such a scale.

Yet how are labor efficiency and material prosperity connected to freedom? An attentive reader of the first chapter of this book may recall that I drew a strict distinction between freedom and material means (a person can be free without property and unfree amidst abundance); at first glance, that might suggest they are unrelated. When we look at the issue in a broader context, however, we find that individuals fighting for their bare survival or the lives of their loved ones are far more likely to take up a weapon intending to rob a neighbor of their resources than those who have enough to eat, a place to sleep (ideally somewhere warm), and who are deciding where to fly for summer vacation. Naturally, this does not mean that materially secure people cannot wage war; it simply means they are less willing to risk their entire existence compared to a situation where their own survival or that of their family is at stake.

Living in material abundance gives us one more fundamental advantage—namely, free time; when we do not have to forage for food in the forest (or toil in the fields) from dawn to dusk, we have room to think and deliberately explore both our inner and outer worlds. In the distant past, our ancestors' survival required accepting countless claims as indisputable facts simply because they were presented as such; they had no time to reflect on them or question them (since practically all their energy went toward securing sustenance), which made them easier to control—a fact eagerly exploited by rulers, churches, and assorted charlatans. Even in modern history we encounter a similar strategy, albeit on a shorter timescale: the Nazis managed to control large numbers of prisoners with relatively few guards in part by keeping them constantly occupied with tasks, sometimes solely so they could not pause, think about their situation, and perhaps devise a plan of resistance or escape. When we have no time to think, we lose our freedom more easily; the more room we gain for reflection, the better our chances of becoming resilient against oppression.

At least as important as sharing material goods, in my view, is the spread of information; as technology advances, the transaction costs of transmitting data keep falling—messengers, carrier pigeons, the printing press, the telegraph, the telephone, radio, television, the internet... As time goes on, we need fewer and fewer resources to learn something. What once required traveling to a library (often distant and not always open to everyone—assuming a person could even read, which just a few hundred years ago the vast majority could not) can today be done simply by reaching into your pocket for a phone and querying an internet search engine or artificial intelligence. In this way, all useful information can spread ever more efficiently—but so can lies, slander, myths, and half-truths; nevertheless, I believe that even if potentially harmful content spreads just as fast as valuable content, lowering the transaction costs of (all) communication will ultimately help freedom more than hurt it. Why do I think so?

Ludwig von Mises wrote: "The criterion of truth is that it works even if nobody is prepared to acknowledge it." He was pointing out that certain principles and laws (such as physical or economic ones) hold regardless of whether people know them or believe in them; discovering and understanding them then enables us to navigate the world better (knowledge of physics helps in aviation or electronics, for instance, while economic understanding warns us away from central planning and the like). It follows that in the long run, individuals and communities living in accordance with truth will statistically be more successful than those clinging to delusions. The belief that truth prevails need not rest merely on naive wishful thinking; evolution and game theory back it up as well—mystification is not a winning strategy over the long haul. Yet what does that say about freedom?

Thousands of years ago, rulers could convince their subjects that they were gods on earth; hundreds of years ago, merely that they ruled by divine will; decades ago, at least that people needed a fully centrally planned economy (though no longer with references to religion); today, even that illusion is gradually crumbling, though it still holds out in certain fields. The better humanity's access to information, the harder it becomes to control us through mystification by those in power. It is hard to imagine literate people with easy access to the knowledge we possess today believing a pharaoh's claim to a supernatural divine nature. Being informed therefore increases our degree of (inner and outer) freedom—also because a free, decentralized society is more economically efficient (a detailed explanation can be found in my book Anarcho-Capitalism), a fact proponents of centralization often do not know, and yet learning economics (that is, acquiring information) can lead them right to it.

From the insights above, it follows that regardless of what we believe, sharing our values and convictions will lead toward freedom rather than unfreedom—whether because feedback in dialogue prompts us to reconsider something ourselves, or because we enrich someone else. At times, of course, movement away from freedom also occurs, yet this is less likely than the opposite process—precisely because being informed tends toward freedom rather than the other way around, as explained in the previous paragraphs; and since we have ever more information at our disposal, we can expect to keep moving closer to freedom (much as has happened from the era of the pharaohs through the Middle Ages down to the present day), which I consider an encouraging outlook. How can we help this along? By sharing, engaging in dialogue, and more broadly doing whatever we can to enrich ourselves and others. In keeping with this conviction, I not only claim no intellectual property over any of my work, but also do not gate access to my content (lectures, videos, podcasts, or texts including books) behind payment—everything can be found online on a voluntary-contribution basis; even admission fees for conferences and lectures, whenever I charge any at all, are left purely to the discretion of attendees so that anyone can participate for free. I am not driven to this by altruism, but by the desire to share information, hold a dialogue (even with those who cannot or do not wish to pay), teach and learn, and do my small part to spread freedom as effectively as possible.

name: 19. Practice
text: In this chapter, we will look at concrete endeavors by individuals thanks to which our society is moving toward freedom—and none of them had to run for votes in elections or persuade anyone how they should or should not live. I will describe various activities by different people in different settings; each is completely unique, yet all are united by the spirit of disobedience. On closer inspection, we will find they have even more in common, which we will explore further in the following chapter; there I will try to show, through the examples of such individuals and projects, how every reader could bring more practical freedom into their own life. For the greatest possible clarity, I have chosen initiatives in which I directly participate, actively collaborate, or at least receive plenty of firsthand information about from their creators over a long period. I will not write about ones that are now (almost or completely) inactive, even if I used to be involved in them (such as Svoboda učení, the Czech and Slovak Ludwig von Mises Institute, the Libertarian Institute, or Prague's Paralelní Polis), nor about ones that are still active but that I do not know deeply enough (the Institute of Liberal Studies, the Liberal Institute, Paralelní Polis branches outside Prague, or countless anarchist or libertarian organizations, agoras, and self-directed schools around the world).

chapter: 19. Practice
name: Hedgehog Without a Cage
text:
Gabriela Ježková did not want to send "her" children to a school where someone would teach them to obey; in 2014, she therefore chose instead to found one herself—a school with neither subordinates nor superiors, no formal hierarchy, and instead equal treatment of children and adults, leaving room for self-direction. A few years later, she asked whether I would like to teach (and learn) there as well; as an enthusiastic theorist in the field of (un)freedom and education, I simply could not turn down such an offer—the chance to experience in practice the principles I had spent years discovering and thinking through ended up exceeding all my high expectations. Not to mention that over time, Hedgehog Without a Cage became my family, a place where I can live freely, be myself, make mistakes, and be accepted (mistakes and all) for exactly who I am. Without Hedgehog (and Gabriela), this book probably would never have come into being either, as I was able to put its ideals into words thanks to the experiences gained at this self-directed school (and also thanks to sharing my life with Gabriela, to whom I also owe the continual expansion of the horizons of my disobedience).

Let us start from the beginning, though. When Gabriela invited me to come teach (and learn) at Hedgehog Without a Cage, that did not mean I could start right away, because neither she nor anyone else can simply decide such a thing on their own; ahead of me lay the longest job interview of my life—it lasted several days straight, during which nobody asked anything of me and I was given no assignments: "Just be here with us however you want and need." This tends to be confusing for people (we bring in both kids and adults the same way) who expect instructions; I, on the other hand, felt right at home—I sat in on a few classes, offered a couple myself, and spent enjoyable time (including evenings and overnight stays at the school) with interesting people. Everyone had a chance to spend time with me and get to know me a little, since my acceptance required the consensus of everyone involved—if even a single person (whether the founder or a first-grader) were opposed, at Hedgehog a majority cannot outvote them. Anyone (which naturally includes both adults and kids) can propose that someone join us (in my case it happened to be Gabriela, since we already knew each other); whether to accept someone, however, is something we all decide together.

We do not seek consensus only when welcoming new hedgehogs; rather, we require it for every decision that at least one of us considers important. No one is obligated to take part in the process (absolutely everything at Hedgehog—including attendance—is voluntary), yet whoever joins in has the opportunity, among other options, to give any proposal a "big yes" or a "big no"—and those cannot be outvoted; if opposing voices like that arise on an issue, we do not close it until we find a solution acceptable to everyone involved. This path can be (and sometimes is) quite demanding—in terms of time, energy, emotions, and relationships—but it is so worthwhile that I wouldn't hesitate to call it one of the core essences of Hedgehog. Not only does it teach all of us to communicate our needs and listen to the needs of others (in a democracy you need to win over a majority, so it pays to persuade the undecided rather than trying to find common ground with people holding opposite views—which is, of course, precisely what consensus requires), but above all it deepens everyone's conviction that their voice matters too. It truly matters. It is not drowned out by a majority, silenced by someone higher up in a hierarchy, lost to rounding during vote tallies, or dismissed because of the speaker's young age. All of this is imprinted on each of us (especially in early childhood) just as powerfully as forced obedience, only with the opposite sign; if we want to live in a genuinely free society, we need to set aside our fears and grant freedom even to the youngest among us.

We likewise create all of our rules through consensus decision-making; we actually have quite a few of them at Hedgehog—they make living together easier. Since we reject all punishments on principle (which wouldn't make much sense in a non-hierarchical environment anyway), no sanction follows for breaking any rule; besides, anyone can challenge any rule at any time, at which point consensus no longer holds for it and a new one must be sought. Rules thus function as guidelines or best practices. Everyone who is interested takes part in shaping them, to the extent they feel comfortable with; from this comes a relatively strong tendency to follow the rules voluntarily—on the one hand, breaking them isn't some "cool" act of rebellion when there is no threat of punishment, and above all, they are our rules, not dictated to us "from above." Because I have been studying polycentric law (that is, the decentralized creation of shared norms "from below") for roughly twenty years, I have visited dozens of schools similar to Hedgehog in order to learn how they create rules; those observations likewise confirm the conclusions above. Watching how processes work at those schools, however, led me to the surprising realization that the manner in which rules are codified also matters greatly. Putting them in writing often causes people, when resolving disputes, to focus on the letter of the rule rather than its spirit, whereas passing them down orally without written records (which is how we do it at Hedgehog) not only eliminates that problem, but also allows unnecessary rules to fade away simply by being forgotten—greatly reducing the burden of being bound by old rules that have lost their purpose without anyone noticing.

The foundational pillars of Hedgehog are freedom, responsibility, and respect—three sides of the same coin; usually only two are mentioned, while we forget about the edge. Because our rules rest on consensus, any one of us can question them at any time, which we consider desirable. This leads, among other things, to complete voluntariness in all activities (including attendance itself), an absence of bans, and equality between kids and adults ("teachers" and "students" have an equal say in deciding anything—no one gives others assignments, grades, or any other evaluation unless explicitly asked to); directly tied to this is the lack of formal hierarchies. Such a setup naturally conflicts with current (adultist) legislation; yet laws can be bent (for example, they require schools to evaluate pupils; nowhere, however, does it say students cannot receive whatever evaluation they choose for themselves) or broken (for instance, I am not allowed to teach kids how to drive or shoot at a school event; yet their wishes—and of course their safety—matter more to me than state regulations), which is precisely the path to achieving freedom discussed in the Liberation chapter. I view Hedgehog as a vivid example of an anarchist agora, even though its members (and formerly myself included) do not think of it that way, and Gabriela certainly did not found it to defy the state or change society—she simply wanted freedom for "her" children.

Certainly not everyone at Hedgehog considers themselves an anarchist; in fact, I would say those of us who do are a minority. Yet I believe every hedgehog understands on some level how unique, free, respectful, and loving a space we create together; and we achieve this—as well as the protection of our way of life—precisely by following the peaceful anarchist principles of disobedience, autonomy, voluntariness, and nonviolence. In the end, practice not only confirms the theory, but even guides toward it those who do not know it or disagree with it. Even though some people at our school view the state as a necessity (or even something good) and consider elections or politics important (though I estimate there are probably even fewer of those than anarchists), they too perceive the absurdity of the Education Act and see the harm that obeying it would bring us. When I talk with them about it, I notice shifts in their attitudes; at least for some of them, over time the fear or guilt that failing to follow legislation is somehow wrong begins to ease.

Hedgehog's approach to children (and not only to them) yields remarkable results—especially when they live in a similar environment at home. I do not want to talk right now about outcomes in acquiring standard school knowledge (though I am convinced self-directed individuals certainly come away with no less of it—rather, it is tailored to their interests—a detailed analysis goes beyond the scope of this book), but rather about being in touch with one's own needs, expressing them, communication skills, and above all the self-confidence that breeds an inclination to disobey empty authority and a natural assumption of responsibility for one's own life—which are the best prerequisites for inner (and subsequently outer) freedom. Between "our" kids and pupils at other schools where I sometimes give talks, I notice a yawning gulf. If I had to generalize and sum it up in a few words, I would probably say that the former live for themselves out of love for life and the world, while the latter strive out of fear to meet other people's expectations; naturally there are exceptions on both sides, yet the overall contrast strikes me immediately. When I see all those unique, autonomous beings at our school who might otherwise have been ground down in the traditional state education system, I feel a deep sense of purpose in what we do—and gratitude to Gabriela, whom I consider my hero for founding this school despite every obstacle (legislative and otherwise): it was the first of its kind in Czechia, yet many more followed, and today there are already dozens like it.

Freedom, self-direction, self-development, sharing—all this and much more is what Hedgehog Without a Cage means to me.

chapter: 19. Practice
name: Free Port
text:
At school, they told me I "didn't know how to learn"—and by what they meant by that, I truly didn't: I didn't enjoy listening to fairly superficial explanations of miscellaneous material in forty-five-minute blocks and then memorizing everything by heart. Even back then, it suited me much better to focus on one area of knowledge or one specific problem at a time and explore it deeply and intensively over a long period, rather than scattering my attention across different topics. Yet out of all the ways of learning and educational models—each of which suits someone different—state schooling forces just a few on everyone while ignoring the rest. That's why it wasn't until sometime after finishing university that I realized with surprise that perhaps I learn most effectively through dialogue: I wrote texts about what interested me, published them online, and discussed them with readers in the comments. Their criticism (often quite harsh, even vulgar) served as fuel for further work; not only did it improve my writing, communication, argumentation, and logical thinking, but I also found it incomparably easier this way (compared to rote cramming) to remember practically any information. For many years I published articles on the website of the Ludwig von Mises Institute and on the D-FENS blog (some of which formed the basis of my first book), until in 2015 I had the idea to start my own web platform called Sewers of the Free Port.

About a year later, communicating with readers inspired me to start making videos and launch a YouTube channel; the name practically suggested itself—Free Port Channel. Over time, my work caught the attention of more people, who expressed interest in lectures on these topics, and those in turn gave rise to more videos. I began traveling around the Czech Republic and Slovakia, speaking at conferences, in schools (which I still consider one of the most important activities), and in various debates, and even reached mainstream media—all despite openly declaring anarchist positions, which well-known anarchists often avoid so as not to be taken for fools (whereas authenticity suits me). Thanks to the support of many followers, Free Port Studio was eventually born, where I still hold discussions with interesting guests today. In addition to financial support from voluntary donors, all these activities require collaborators; and so Free Port was founded—an association whose purpose lies primarily in opening the broadest possible dialogue on freedom, encompassing anarchy, economics, ethics, and the free market, though over time education has emerged as one of our most prominent themes.

Free Port obviously reaches orders of magnitude fewer children than state schooling; nevertheless, I know of hundreds whom it has significantly influenced (above all through the topic of disobedience or the realization that when they don't fit school and school doesn't fit them, the problem doesn't have to lie with them)—and I'm still in touch with many of them. In connection with self-directed education, the House of the Free Port was also established: a property in northern Bohemia consisting of meadows, a small forest, a garden, and several buildings, where a community of people spontaneously formed to organize all kinds of events focused on free learning (originally it was SvobodUm of the association Svoboda učení, where I spent several years as one of the project's creators until Free Port eventually bought it). Although these activities are meant for anyone regardless of age, they naturally attract heightened interest from children and parents, which makes me very happy: every person who doesn't have to grow up in obedience represents a greater chance for a slightly freer society.

Among our other work, I consider important the annual Free Port Conference on various topics related to freedom (we have already organized seven of them), the illegal #ne_poslušnosti ("disobedience") actions carried out in a spirit of respect for people and public disrespect for state laws, the candidacy of the Nevolte Urza.cz ("Don't Vote Urza.cz") party in elections (aimed at spreading anarchist ideas in pre-election public debate, though with a binding pledge to refuse without hesitation any political offices or public budget funds if we were to win any), creating a comic, and, last but not least, publishing this book. It makes me happy whenever any of it inspires someone or otherwise enriches their life, so I try to distribute all content freely online, where over the years it has reached hundreds of thousands of people (even if many disagree with it or are outright outraged by it). Still, I create primarily to fulfill my own need to learn and grow, which is more important to me than potential effects on other people (and, by extension, society as a whole)—an insight I consider essential for the next chapter.

chapter: 19. Practice
name: Cryptomoney
text:
In late 2008, a person or group of people using the pseudonym Satoshi Nakamoto defined the protocol for the open-source peer-to-peer payment network Bitcoin; it was launched in January 2009, initially serving as a toy for a handful of enthusiasts. A year and a half later, someone used it for a purchase for the first time—programmer Laszlo Hanyecz ordered two pizzas for 10,000 BTC, little suspecting at the time that a few years later cryptoanarchists would begin celebrating May 22 as "Pizza Day" in honor of that transaction. Today, for the same number of bitcoins, we could buy, say, a large private island with a luxury palace, power plant, airport, harbor, private jet, helicopter, yacht, and maybe even a submarine—and we wouldn't have to worry much about the budget, either, as plenty would be left over for operating costs for the rest of our lives. Why has the price risen so astronomically? Because more and more people understand that Bitcoin is a great store of value—far better than any current state currency (which, by contrast, lose value due to their inflationary nature).

From a (crypto)anarchist perspective, I see the absence of any central authority as Bitcoin's most important feature: it is a decentralized network that anyone can join at any time and begin participating in running. Whereas balances in ordinary bank accounts are managed by banks (which therefore have the ability to freeze them and the like), all Bitcoin transactions—including the complete history—are simultaneously stored by tens of thousands of computers spread around the world; and if one of them happens to decide to block my funds, a request to transfer them will simply be processed by another. Detractors claim that the intelligence agencies of some superpower might be hiding behind the pseudonym Satoshi Nakamoto, which I don't consider very likely; however, the beauty of decentralization lies above all in the fact that it is completely irrelevant—even if it were true, Bitcoin's creator has no actual power over it (and not even a backdoor, since it is software with publicly accessible open source code).

Conversely, I consider Bitcoin's greatest weakness to be that it is not fully anonymous: while it doesn't show who owns which funds, their transfers can be tracked—the history of all transactions is public (although they cannot be linked to specific individuals without additional information, states are gradually beginning to spend more and more resources to obtain that "additional information"). While this problem can usually be addressed somehow to protect one's privacy, doing so requires an advanced understanding of how the entire network works as well as blockchain analysis tools—not to mention that anyone can simply make a mistake, as a result of which, unfortunately, quite a few seasoned cryptoanarchists have seen the inside of a prison cell. In response to this, projects like Monero were created—which can be thought of as Bitcoin's "younger brother" that operates in complete anonymity, where no one can track another person's transactions without the author's permission; that's also why it is commonly used on illegal darknet markets (though it has other limitations of its own). For completeness, I should note that Bitcoin has tens of thousands of various "siblings"; almost without exception, these are non-functional or outright fraudulent projects in which you can easily sink your savings—yet their existence provides much-needed competition that separates the wheat from the chaff (and even so, I consider some of them more trustworthy than state currencies).

When I wrote the chapter on money in my book *Anarcho-Capitalism* in 2013, I didn't mention a single word about Bitcoin; although I knew of its existence, its amazing potential remained hidden to me at the time (for about two years). Far more prescient was my friend Slush: already in late 2010, he came up with the world's first implementation of a mining pool (software used for collective confirmation of transactions on the network) and subsequently, in 2014, with the Trezor—the world's first hardware wallet (a device capable of securely storing bitcoins). I don't know who Satoshi Nakamoto was or why they did what they did; Slush, however, told me about his motivations—he initially developed these technologies for his own use, because he enjoyed it. Later, his companies broke through on the global market and their products helped millions of people (myself included) expand the boundaries of their financial freedom for just a few (thousand) crowns; yet that probably never even crossed his mind in the earliest days of exploring Bitcoin—an observation we will return to in the next chapter.

chapter: 19. Practice
name: Cryptoanarchy
text:
Cryptomoney, however, is only the publicly known tip of a vast iceberg born of cryptoanarchism; the term was first coined by Timothy Christopher May in *The Crypto Anarchist Manifesto*, which he circulated to the cypherpunk community back in 1988. The message of that manifesto is that strong asymmetric cryptography can weaken state power—and not politically, but technologically: politicians may write laws, yet the mathematics of encryption algorithms will not submit to them. Even before the invention of web technology, Timothy C. May predicted a world in which we would be able to communicate and trade anonymously, transfer funds outside the banking system, and enter into contracts without an official identity; all of this came true within a few decades. In 1994, he described cryptoanarchy as the practical realization of anarcho-capitalism in cyberspace. I completely agree with that, and would only refine the claim further: in my view, it is specifically the realization of anarchoagorism, since it emerges "from below," undirected by anyone, without any central plan or political will.

Today's cryptoanarchists have a vast array of technologies at their disposal, from diverse algorithms and computer networks to very powerful hardware; thanks to this, they can create communities in cyberspace with relative ease. Whereas in the past one could hardly belong to a tribe without being physically present, modern technologies allow us to do so, enabling a return to (cyber)tribalism; at the same time, tribes don't have to exist solely virtually—they are often tied to a specific location in the physical world (I myself belong to agoras separated physically by hundreds of kilometers, so I live in multiple places, travel between them, and yet thanks to the internet continue to take part in their functioning). Such relationships—personal, creative, educational, commercial, professional, advisory, supportive, charitable, and more—strengthen the decentralization of society, especially when forged by individuals who do not require external authorities supervising their lives; in cryptographically secured privacy (and, where needed, pseudonymity or complete anonymity), they can interact autonomously and freely without excessive risk of retaliation from the state.

chapter: 19. Practice
name: Rainbow Family of Living Light
text:
The Rainbow Family emerged in 1970 as an offshoot of the hippie movement at the American music festival Vortex I (a smaller Oregonian version of the famous Woodstock). Today it is a worldwide informal, non-hierarchical organization likely numbering hundreds of thousands of people (there is no official membership list, though some gatherings have drawn tens of thousands at once). Its core values are love, peace, freedom, voluntariness, respect for people and nature, spiritual openness, sharing, and equality (in the sense of shared humanity, not material or other egalitarianism); in keeping with these values, they have no leaders, operating instead in nonviolent decentralized self-governments. They make all decisions by consensus, which with large numbers of people can sometimes take a long time; yet (much like at Hedgehog Without a Cage) it brings a range of advantages—above all, genuine peaceful problem-solving without suppressing those whose voices happen not to be loud enough.

The Rainbow Family's most visible events are Rainbow Gatherings, held in nature around the world and lasting a month (beginning at the new moon, peaking at the full moon, and ending at the next new moon). At any given moment, a Rainbow Gathering is taking place somewhere in the world (often in several places at once); some members of this family travel from one gathering to the next so that it makes up their entire lives, others spend part of the year that way, and others drop by occasionally. At such an event, thousands of people may gather in one (carefully chosen) spot—Rainbow Family scouts speak with locals in advance, inform them about the gathering, and gauge their views (if the response is negative, they look for another site); if the piece of land has a private owner, their consent is a non-negotiable condition. On public (state) land, permits matter far less; this occasionally leads to police interventions of varying scale and intensity, to which the (often naked) hippies always react the same way—treating the intervening officers as rainbow sisters and brothers (since that is how they treat everyone who comes to a Rainbow Gathering), which sometimes resolves the conflict through nonviolent communication, at other times leads to the area being completely cleared by police force, and more often to its being cordoned off (though guarding kilometers of dense forest non-stop for a month is no easy task even for dozens of patrols, so it is easy to slip in and out, as Gabriela and I once experienced firsthand in Germany). Such interventions are quite rare, however; typically it is a serene meeting of peaceful hippies who celebrate the full moon, clean up meticulously after themselves (there is heavy emphasis on this), and scatter to all corners of the globe (or on to the next gathering). They don't need permission to live their own way; nor do they fight anyone for it—they simply do it.

chapter: 19. Practice
name: Liberation Travel
text:
About ten years ago, the smiling digital nomad, (crypto)anarchist, voluntarist, and ethical hacker Pavol "Wilder" Lupták entered my life; our meetings and conversations are a great inspiration to me, not only for his unfailing good-natured warmth and kindness, but also for his flagrant disobedience toward imposed authorities, to whom he has spent virtually his whole life (with his characteristic peacefulness and gentleness, yet completely unyieldingly) showing a metaphorical raised middle finger. Palo loves to travel; and on his travels he noticed vast differences in how individual states treat "their" citizens in various areas, which he decided to turn to his advantage—in one country he arranged citizenship, in another tax residency for his company, elsewhere permanent residency, while paying for his health insurance with a private global insurer. As a result, his children don't even legally have to attend school, the authorities have a hard time keeping tabs on him since he is constantly on the move, and collecting taxes from him isn't exactly easy either (among other reasons, because he uses crypto—especially anonymous Monero—more than state currencies); yet I am quite sure his motivation is not greed (on the contrary, he generously helps those in need), but a desire for freedom and autonomy.

When he began sharing what he had learned with others, he inspired so many anarchists (and other freedom-minded people) that they decided to follow in his footsteps. Palo wasted no time and founded Liberation Travel—a professional agency that can arrange permanent residency (and eventually perhaps citizenship) for you in places like Panama, Uruguay, or Paraguay, freeing you from hefty taxes in Europe or the US, or set up a bank account in Georgia or Kyrgyzstan that does not report banking data to the tax authorities of other countries. What I love is that although Liberation Travel naturally charges fees for handling the bureaucracy, Palo still continuously shares all the necessary information completely free of charge to help people live freely; he actively uses all these services himself all the time, so in the relevant countries and elsewhere on his travels he keeps track of legislative changes, not only adapting to them himself but also constantly publishing his findings for free online and at conferences around the world. This anarchist didn't set out on a mission to save the world or society either; he simply loves traveling and found his path to freedom in it—and only then offered it to others.

chapter: 19. Practice
name: Students for Liberty
text: Students for Liberty is—as the name suggests—a libertarian student organization; it was founded in 2008 at a conference of the same name in New York, from which it quickly spread far beyond the United States—today it brings together over ten thousand students in more than a thousand chapters practically all over the world. Its members collaborate on organizing lectures, conferences, debate evenings, and informal meetups; they also publish books, and when needed they don't hesitate to help their members and their loved ones flee war-torn regions. The Czech branch was founded in 2013 in Brno, from where it expanded to many other cities; and since the local libertarian community ranks globally among the most active (and per capita even among the largest), it is not all that surprising that Students for Liberty CZ won the award for best student group at the SFL Awards. I have collaborated with many of their members for years and we help one another out (for example, with promoting this book, but also with things like sheltering people pursued by the immigration police). They are typically kind-hearted, respectful young people who enjoy listening, talking, reading, and writing about freedom, so they built a platform where they can do so. I greatly enjoy speaking at events organized by this group because they take place in a very friendly, loving atmosphere full of understanding and tolerance even for differing opinions; I feel no pressure from the participants to change anyone (whether specific individuals or society as a whole)—on the contrary, rather humility and a desire to broaden their own horizons.

chapter: 19. Practice
name: Agora
text:
One of Prague's agoras is called simply "Agora" by its members; although I'm a big fan of names that are as descriptive as possible, I find this one slightly confusing. Still, its work encompasses quite a wide spectrum of freedom-related activities—both in the physical and digital worlds; and because I appreciate both the diversity and the independence of these expressions of disobedience, I'll briefly introduce each of them.

The idea at Agora that intrigued me the most is connecting anarchists of all stripes—from anarcho-capitalists to anarcho-communists—on common ground, which we may gradually be finding in anarchoagorism. I believe this "center" could be a meeting point for everyone willing to put their anarchist ideals ahead of hostility toward unfamiliar differences that they are often not even willing to understand. I myself have been trying—unsuccessfully—to foster a similar dialogue among anarchists for many years; and I would dearly love for the key to it to lie in this very agora.

Another contribution of these anarchists to freedom, in my view, is a project they also named Agora (presumably so nothing gets confused). It is a decentralized protocol for the digital representation of relationships and events (both within agoras and between them), enabling them to manifest online without involuntary data sharing or the need for a central authority. To achieve this, it uses asymmetric cryptography and blockchain technology, which in recent years—as it grew popular—has very often been implemented senselessly; however, I find its use in Agora genuinely functional, since its creators account for the so-called "oracle problem"—while of course they cannot solve it completely, they significantly mitigate its effects. For anyone who finds this paragraph too technical, you can picture Agora as an encrypted "app" through which members of different agoras can communicate both internally and with other agoras, plan, trade, make agreements, and do many other things, as each agora can customize this "app" to its own needs without losing the ability to communicate with the rest. Since Agora isn't quite finished yet, I'm not sure whether it will be released before or after this book; however, I find its development team quite open (they gladly welcomed my suggestions and feedback on their work)—so if you feel like it, you can try getting involved as well.

In addition, Agora manages Autonomous Center 254 in Prague's Holešovice district—a space for individuals and collectives aligned with anarchist ideas. It brings together a colorful range of people, from Bitcoiners to artists to the Salvation Army; the members of AC254 place emphasis on solidarity, which shows, among other things, in voluntary pay-what-you-want prices for the food and drinks available there. Personally, I most enjoy dropping by "two-five-four" to chat about interesting topics related to freedom, though it also hosts various educational and cultural events; I fell in love with the place and the people in it fairly quickly—although we don't always agree on everything, they are open to dialogue, and above all I strongly sense that they care far more about whether an action is right or wrong than whether it is legal or illegal, which is an attitude that makes it possible to build a truly autonomous space.

chapter: 19. Practice
name: Smugglers, dealers, whores, and other free outlaws
text:
There is a wide range of services and commodities on which states slap special taxes or outlaw altogether—mostly foreign goods, drugs, weapons, sex, and the like. The original (and often ongoing) reasons for such restrictions typically relate to centralizing power, filling public coffers, populism (and not only before elections), or even racism. Bizarre or conspiratorial as it may sound today, the history of drug prohibition, for instance, stretches back to the nineteenth century, when politicians did not hesitate to play the racist card quite openly; if you look into the origins of banning cocaine, opium, marijuana, and especially peyote, you might be surprised. Today, the existence of those identical regulations is routinely defended on grounds of health or safety even where such arguments don't stand up to scrutiny beyond first glance (which I examine in detail in my book *Anarcho-Capitalism* as well as in lectures on drugs and weapons, recordings of which can be found on the Free Port Channel on YouTube or Odysee). Understandably, though, the vast majority of people have neither the time nor the motivation to examine the sensibility of these measures more deeply, so they automatically adopt the state's positions and rationales portraying such restrictions as necessary and beneficial to society.

As a result of these majority opinions, anyone who—contrary to current legislation—supplies others with goods they demand is condemned across the board; and not so much according to the actual danger of the item in question, but above all according to society-wide prejudices—distributors of any illegal drugs are frequently blamed with relish by all sorts of moralizers for the negative effects of their wares on consumers' health, yet in my life I have never heard anyone blame a bartender or a corner-store clerk for an alcoholic's liver cirrhosis. Naturally, among smugglers and dealers (not only of drugs) we also find plenty of real criminals who don't shrink from stealing or otherwise infringing on the rights and freedoms of others. Purely statistically, moreover, we encounter them in these professions more often than in the general population, since the very illegality of such businesses deters, for instance, people with strong risk aversion or a high need for social approval (and for those very traits, there will be fewer thieves, aggressors, and the like among them). None of that changes the fact, however, that plenty of decent, honest people who neither rob nor otherwise harm anyone make their living selling drugs, (untaxed) sex, and engaging in other taboo or outright illegal trades—yet society looks down its nose at them.

Under such social pressure, these individuals often come to view themselves as outcasts; not infrequently (owing in part to the need to conceal their work), they eventually start believing they are doing something wrong, even though they are often merely supplying people with goods and services they want. Their biggest "offense" typically consists either in selling something politicians say they shouldn't sell (even in the case of goods with negligible or negative harmfulness), or in refusing to share potential profits with state authorities, or simply in being unwilling to submit to their demands to follow nonsensical standards or red tape. Yet whenever they take this path (even from purely selfish motives), in my eyes they push our society toward freedom. I'm glad for everyone who finds enough courage to do their work without permission, regardless of legislation, without handing part of their earnings over to the state, guided solely by the desire to make things better for themselves or others (while respecting them). Thanks to technology, such individuals can now also meet anonymously on darknet marketplaces—which tend to be a thorn in the side (and a target of aggression) of governments worldwide, because they weaken state power by letting people conveniently obtain high-quality items over which state organs would love to usurp a monopoly.

I regard all honest smugglers, dealers, whores (I use this word with great respect and appreciation), and other free outlaws as important allies on the path to practical anarchy; I respect them for their disobedience and willingness to live autonomously on their own terms regardless of what authorities demand. I let them know this attitude of mine, so around me they are typically not ashamed to talk about their work (including its illegal aspects). That often provides a great springboard for introducing them to relevant insights from the Austrian school of economics or various anarchist theories, which they usually enjoy hearing—thanks to these ideas, they can view what they do as a useful service to others rather than some despicable hustle at someone's expense, as the state shamefully insinuates. I know personally (and in some cases very well) many dealers in illegal goods and sex workers in the gray economy; quite a few of them felt ashamed of their livelihood for various reasons—sometimes so much so that they planned to earn some money and switch to making an "honest" living. Yet after grasping the principles of anarchoagorism (and receiving support from other like-minded people), they often abandoned those plans. Part of the purpose of some agoras can simply be helping their members feel accepted in a world whose majority unfortunately rejects them just as they are. On the road to freedom, we don't only run into legislative obstacles; we often have to deal with prejudices and social norms as well.

name: 20. Participation
text:
Over the many years I've been spreading ideas of freedom in the public sphere, people have come to me from time to time (and, happily, more and more often) with the following prompt: "All right, Urza, after thinking it through carefully, I agree that I don't need any rulers; but we live in the here and now. What good does it do me to understand that the state is robbing me of my freedom? It happens whether I'm aware of it or not. What can I realistically do about it?" The purpose of this book is to answer precisely such questions. In its first part, I describe how and why we lose our freedom; next comes an analysis of paths that do not lead to regaining it; the preceding chapter, however, is the longest of all—it documents concrete activities of individual people through which they themselves (and subsequently others) can live more freely. Let's learn something from them. How do their stories differ? And what, on the other hand, do they have in common?

The protagonists of our practical examples come from completely different backgrounds and, at first glance, live entirely different lives—from a mother with children to (digital) creators, (crypto)anarchists, hackers, and even hippies, all the way to dealers and whores (I still use that word with great respect and appreciation). So what unites them? Certainly a desire for freedom, of which they had less than they needed at the start of their journey—whether it was the obligation to send their children to a dreadful state school, the central banks' monopoly on money, the requirement to pay taxes, or the illegality of certain goods or services. Many people simply accept this, resign themselves to it, and at most go to the pub or online to complain about the state of our society or the times we live in; that attitude corresponds to the victim mindset I wrote about in the *Self-Development* chapter. The individuals above, however, chose to act as conscious creators (of their own lives); they didn't ask for permission—respecting the freedom of others, they went after what they needed, in spite of every social or legal norm.

Yet that's not all; these people share one more crucial trait: their primary goal is not to save society, rescue the world, or even "do good"—not that they are indifferent to others, but their driving force is not a need to change other people. I also know plenty of similarly active and hardworking "freedom fighters" whose foremost desire, however, is to be heroes, improve social conditions, advance justice, or at least liberate the weak or ignorant; yet I included none of them in the previous chapter, because over time they all either burned out or gradually abandoned their ideals—this happens primarily in politics, of course, though sometimes outside it too, since people oriented toward the external world more easily succumb to peer pressure and become obedient, for instance in chasing followers on social media (speaking out publicly that we consider children our equals, for example, isn't nearly as popular as talking about creating a safe environment for the most vulnerable).

What, then, forms the driving force behind the actions of the protagonists in the previous chapter, if not an effort to improve or liberate society? The answer is quite simple: thanks to their inner freedom, they simply do what they enjoy and what fulfills them.
