If you saw Gabriela surrounded by the kids from Hedgehog, Slush working tirelessly at SatoshiLabs, naked hippies carrying firewood to the fire at a Rainbow Gathering, Palo on his travels, or my own enthusiasm while writing literally every sentence of this book, you wouldn't be witnessing efforts to change the world, but people living out things that give them meaning and that they do gladly and with love. They walk the path to their own freedom, impose it on no one, and simply share their knowledge and experience with others, leaving it entirely up to them whether they want to follow or not. Because there is no universal solution for everyone, it makes little sense to focus on society as a whole, which tends to be just an escape from oneself anyway—whereas changing ourselves is, in the end, the only thing we can effectively do.

For that reason, there is no place for social engineering on my path to freedom, and I renounce every means that is inconsistent with my goal—for no end justifies it. As long as we are not free on the inside (and are afraid to do what fulfills us), we cannot very well expand (and above all sustain over the long term) external freedom either. The more (unprocessed) fear we carry within us, the more easily we fall into the trap of various compromises and concessions along the way (especially in the most sensitive and at the same time most critical areas—such as limiting the autonomy of children). Let's start with ourselves and force nothing on anyone; if it makes sense to others, they will join on their own. One beauty of this approach is that when someone gets something wrong, they mainly bear the consequences themselves; by contrast, the mistakes of social engineers (both statist and libertarian, when they try to implement freedom "from above") are typically paid for by almost everyone, even those who disagree with their methods.

What specifically can you personally do for freedom? Whenever I want to bring something new into my life, I start minimalistically and add on only gradually; I find that far more effective than making grand plans, dreaming up castles in the air, and then discovering it doesn't actually suit me. So let's take a look at some small practical first steps toward freedom; I don't expect all of them to suit anyone, yet I also doubt you won't find at least a few among them to use as a starting point:

• If you start communicating using encryption (today I'd recommend the secure Signal app, which requires no digital literacy), you'll make it significantly harder for anyone (especially state authorities) to snoop on your communications. Nor do you need to be a rocket scientist to use a VPN or Tor—even if you're hearing these terms for the first time, you only need to type them into a search engine or ask an AI about them to get a basic grasp in a few (dozen) minutes. Why hide if you have nothing to hide, you ask? Well, the more people use such tools, the less suspicious they look (plus their adoption rate in society grows, which matters for something like Signal, for example)—not to mention that as you follow further points on this list, you might come to appreciate digital privacy.

• If you earn even a little more money than the bare subsistence minimum, you can save something every month; you can almost always live a bit more modestly. Many working-age people steadily spend their entire income; yet nearly everyone can spend a few (or a few dozen) percent less—just stop comparing your material options with richer people, because you almost certainly know someone around you who gets by on a little less, meaning you probably can too. Why is saving so important? Savings increase your independence—not just from your boss or clients, but above all from the state. It has the audacity to rob "its" citizens of most of their income and then tell them that without it they wouldn't be provided for in old age; you don't have to buy into that, though. Who is easier to control: a penniless retiree, or one with ten million in crypto, stocks, real estate, or commodities? Which of them is a politician more likely to buy off with promises? And which one will more easily slip from the creator's stance into the victim role? People often convince themselves they "have to" or "have no other choice" simply because they aren't willing to scale back their lifestyle. Moreover, savings can appreciate (and diversifying them minimizes risk), so you don't even have to set aside quite as much money (assuming, of course, that you don't save exclusively in state currency, which makes no sense for many reasons). I repeatedly hear that I can only afford my anarchist views because I'm young and healthy; all the harder I work, then, to make sure I can keep them in my old age too.

• With cryptomoney, you can not only save, but above all store value beyond the sight and reach of the state (or anyone else). Don't know how? At krypto.urza.cz you can read everything a newcomer to the crypto world needs to know.

• If you skip taking a receipt when paying in cash (or crypto), you potentially make it easier for some (mainly smaller) vendors to leave that transaction untaxed, which can help—even if just a tiny bit—to weaken the state; in some cases you'll save money yourself too. Personally, I do this on principle; I trust that practically anyone I do business with will put that money to better use than a state bureaucrat.

• In general, the less of your money gets taxed, the more of it you get to spend as you see fit—and that holds regardless of how strong a social conscience you have, because everything you don't hand over to the state remains yours to allocate at your discretion (say, to charity or anything else). Some taxes (often indirect ones) I don't know how to avoid; many, however, are enforced based on things the relevant administrative authority doesn't need to know about at all unless someone reports them—and here it matters greatly what kind of people you surround yourself with and do business with, which is something agoras can help with enormously.

• If you learn to deal with representatives of the state (above all police officers) as equals—that is, not from a subordinate position—you'll help yourself first (it won't be so easy to intimidate you and get you to say or do things that end up hurting you), and other people second (subservient behavior toward authorities only emboldens them to overstep further). How to do this and why it matters even when you aren't doing anything wrong (even under current law) is something you can learn in my lecture "Anarcho-Capitalism: How (Not) to Talk to Cops (and Not Only Them)?" (a recording of it is freely available online on the Free Port Channel).

• When you realize that laws are not walls, but more like chalk lines on a playing field that can be stepped over when necessary, new and unexpected possibilities open up before you. I'm not claiming all legislation can be ignored without consequences; some laws can be bent, others broken, many circumvented, and still others have varying (often ambiguous) interpretations, though disrespecting them naturally carries certain risks. It depends on your attitude: you can view legislation as an inviolable boundary (or even as morally right, in which case neither the odds of getting caught nor the severity of potential punishment plays a decisive role), or simply as a list of things the state authority wants (for various reasons) to punish "its" citizens for—and it's entirely up to you how you deal with it. If that feels too risky, you can always start with something carrying a minimal penalty; in time you can get used to anything and gradually stop being afraid.

• Besides laws, social norms can also restrict a person's (especially internal) freedom; violating them won't send you to prison or get you fined, yet you may face condemnation or ostracism (which are legitimate ways for others to express disapproval). Still, once you start being yourself and decide to resist social pressures, some of the people around you may drift away—yet that creates space for people who are genuinely comfortable with who you really are. It may sound harsh and look scary, but the measure of freedom that opens up through such steps is anything but negligible. At first you may face judgment for breaking social norms, yet if you stick with it, over time you'll find yourself surrounded by people who don't mind (either because they learn to accept you as you are, or because they refuse to and leave your circle), which often brings an immense—for many, almost unimaginable—relief.

• Wherever you work, the environment you spend time in inevitably shapes you; someone who serves in the military from eighteen onward will likely have a different temperament and worldview in old age than a hippie who spent their whole life in the Rainbow Family. If, say, you work at a corporation, over time its corporate culture, habits, ways of approaching problems or communicating, and other norms will likely carry over to some degree into your own thinking and lifestyle; formal hierarchies (even voluntary ones, including those in smaller firms) steer people toward obedience more than other environments. Meanwhile, more and more self-managed organizations are emerging (sometimes called "teal"—companies with a very flat structure, essentially without managers); in most fields, freelancing is also an option. I'm not saying you should quit your job tomorrow (especially if you're happy there); I'm merely inviting you to reflect on how much what (and especially where) you do for a living shapes you in terms of freedom, something to keep in mind the next time you make changes in that area.

• Do you have children? Or would you like to have them someday? How you intend to treat them will dramatically affect not only their lives, but your own as well. If you decide to steer them toward goals you consider right and try to actively instill your values in them (other than simply living by those values yourself), you inevitably cast yourself in the commanding role, leaving them in a subordinate position. We examined the consequences of obedience in several chapters at the beginning of this book. If you can view children as equal beings despite their lesser life experience (by which I obviously don't mean equality in abilities or skills), respect their preferences and attitudes (often shaped precisely by that lack of experience), and refrain from teaching them to obey, it will aid not only their growth into autonomous, responsible individuals, but also your own perception of freedom. It is said that the true character of a society is reflected in how it treats its weakest members; I believe the same holds true for the character of individuals—and that children are typically the weakest.

• If none of the points above yet feels imaginable or meaningful to you (or if you want to do even more), you can start following (and perhaps even supporting) Free Port. Not only do we explore these topics in depth there, but we also bring together like-minded individuals from whom one can learn; through direct support, you also help spread these ideas to others.

The options above are not meant to tell anyone how to live their life; I offer them merely as examples to consider for people who have no idea where to begin their journey toward freedom. Even following all of them, however, wouldn't automatically make anyone free; rather, along the way, they gain the opportunity to start thinking differently than they were used to. I don't believe there is a checklist of steps such that once we complete them, we're liberated and done; it's more of a lifestyle—something ongoing that we can continually work on. If we want to live healthily, for instance, it isn't enough to work out once, eat a plate of vegetables, and forget about it; we need to devote time, attention, effort, and energy to it continuously. Freedom is no different: it too requires us to reflect on it, integrate it into our lives, learn to perceive it, and practice experiencing it. The good news is that the more attention we give to freedom, the more natural a part of our everyday lives it becomes. At first it may seem too abstract, yet anyone who allows themselves to weave some of the options above into their daily routine (ideally not just mechanically, but by thinking seriously about them and seeking out relevant information) may after a while see new paths opening up whose existence they previously had no inkling of—typically applying freedom to every major area of life, from work to hobbies to relationships.

If we remain isolated with our values and convictions, we can certainly expand our personal autonomy by changing our actions and thinking in certain areas; sooner or later, however, we will inevitably run into limits stemming not only from a lack of support around us, but also from the absence of a division of labor. In modern society we aren't self-sufficient—we rely on other people's goods and services; yet when those people are statists, they may have no interest in cooperating with us outside the oversight of the state apparatus (unless they happen to want to save a bit on taxes). The solution lies in the previously mentioned agoras: there we can connect with like-minded individuals who share compatible values—and it is an incredible relief to live in an environment where legislation is not treated as an argument for whether an action is right or wrong (at most, we consider how to eliminate or at least mitigate the impact of potential sanctions).

Anyone who doesn't belong to an agora can find one or create one; the more naturally and transparently a person takes the steps toward freedom above (or any others), the more like-minded people will begin to turn up around them. Authenticity is a huge advantage here. I'm sometimes criticized for proclaiming my convictions too openly—supposedly that puts a lot of people off. Yes, it does; I close many doors, since to many people I lose all credibility as a crazy anarchist (unfortunately, even some former libertarian colleagues feel the need to distance themselves from me lest their social status suffer), yet I open plenty of other doors—countless individuals share their disobedience to laws with me, confide all sorts of bizarre troubles with legislation, and we help and advise one another on how to shield ourselves from the power of authorities. Nor do you have to be quite so radical; just let a little more freedom into your life and don't hide it too much—birds of a feather flock together, and in time you'll run into people of a similar mindset. And if nowhere else, just drop by one of Free Port's events; the place is swarming with anarchists.

Although the state apparatus creates the illusion that disobedience (to laws) never goes unpunished (which is unfortunately sometimes true), in the vast majority of cases that is simply not so. As I already mentioned in *The State* chapter, roughly two and a half million legal norms are in force in the Czech Republic, so there is probably no one living on "its" territory who knows all of them (let alone obeys them); I wonder if there is a single person anywhere in the world who knows every law that applies to them. When I try to recall at least one full day when I personally did not knowingly break the law, I have to go back about five years—most of that day I spent in an operating room, and the rest hovering between wakefulness and induced sleep; since waking up, I know of no other such day (nor, for that matter, of ever having harmed or endangered anyone by breaking legislation). Over that entire period, I was detained once and brought to a police station (for violating the State Symbols Act, failing to prove my identity, and subsequently disobeying an official's order) and fined a couple of times (for traffic infractions). I admit I'm not exactly a representative sample of the population, yet there is a dizzying disproportion between the crimes committed (sometimes quite serious from the state's standpoint) and the resulting penalties. I don't mean to say laws can be broken with impunity (after all, plenty of people end up in prison, whether they hurt anyone or not); only that, in my direct and indirect experience, the boundaries of what we can get away with lie significantly farther out than almost everyone (including most anarchists) assumes. One can test this gradually to see what still flies and what doesn't (which naturally carries risks); however, the information gained can be shared in agoras, dramatically lowering the cost of such discovery.

Ultimately, only each individual can judge their own options; some people are highly risk-averse, while others don't mind risky ventures. Still, there are paths to freedom whose level of danger is negligible—or at least comparable to anything else we routinely do. I consider it most important to take (some) first step and think it all through; there is no need to rush anywhere or build castles in the air and grandiose plans for the future. Doing something out of "noble" motives to "change society" often leads to frustration that people aren't what we need them to be. When, however, we stick to what we ourselves enjoy and find fulfilling—with the sole difference that we consciously decide to invite freedom into our lives—we may inspire others along the way; and even if we don't, at the very least we'll enjoy it ourselves. Teachers can seek out or found freer schools, programmers can contribute to the rise of cryptomoney, artists can create works about disobedience, therapists can support children's autonomy, tradespeople and farmers can participate in the gray economy, lawyers can help victimless "criminals," scientists can look for work outside the state sphere... I'm not claiming this is the best advice (and certainly not for everyone); I can do no more than offer examples and point in a rough direction. Once you set out on that road, you yourself will know best what exactly is needed.

name: 21. The Future
text:
Anarchoagorism can be viewed as a practical path to an individual's personal freedom using means accessible to every one of us. Part of its appeal lies in the fact that we can follow it virtually regardless of how (un)free a society we live in; concrete results will of course depend heavily on external conditions—from anarchoagorism practiced inside a prison, it is obviously unrealistic to expect the degree of freedom common on the other side of the walls and bars, yet increasing one's freedom is certainly still possible. The practical steps described in the previous chapter are designed for most people in today's Euro-Atlantic civilization; some apply universally, while others depend on local conditions. From the general principles of anarchoagorism—which can be described, very simplistically, as voluntary cooperation among the disobedient without formal authorities—anyone can deduce specific measures and practices for their own life anytime and anywhere. Putting them into practice then not only increases an individual's degree of freedom, but also teaches them to discover further steps on this path, whose implementation leads to still more, and so on.

Although I consider one of this book's key messages to be its call to bring about change "from below" (each starting with themselves) rather than "from above" (authoritatively toward others), I would be surprised if some readers didn't wonder how anarchoagorism might affect society as a whole. Before exploring this topic further, I'd like to note that while the broader social reach of this philosophy can be imagined and modeled in various ways, we must keep in mind the pitfalls of doing so: the more we focus our attention on other people and the outside world, the more easily we lose sight of working on ourselves. I'm not discouraging anyone from analyzing the global impacts of anarchoagorism across populations; I do believe, however, that (in any action) motive matters greatly: when we strive to achieve our own freedom (and help only those who actually want it), we naturally become conscious creators (of our lives) in the process, whereas attempts to change society often end in the victim role, where the spurned "savior" feels misunderstood and frustrated that others don't grasp his ideas and don't follow him (from which it is an easy slide into disrespecting and coercing others on the grounds that they don't know what's good for them anyway). Please read the following lines with full awareness of everything mentioned in this paragraph...

In the *New Libertarian Manifesto*, Samuel Edward Konkin III describes several phases of revolution (which I, however, would call evolution): it begins in a state where no one follows the anarchoagorist path (phase zero); continues with its adoption by a handful of libertarians in an otherwise statist society (phase one); their numbers gradually grow until state power takes notice and can not only punish individual disobedients, but also attempt widespread intimidation (phase two); if central authorities fail to stamp out the agoras, their supercritical growth threatens the establishment due to ever larger shortfalls in tax revenues, while parallel structures grow stronger for the same reason—up to the point where they can defend themselves against a potential attack by the former oppressor's armed forces (phase three); and with the loss of its monopoly on violence, the state ceases to be a state (phase four). In his manifesto, SEK3 examines each phase in greater detail (including an analysis of potential risks); yet even though I broadly agree with him and find his account of the path to freedom plausible, it makes little sense to me today to devise a strategy for changing a future society we do not live in—and thus cannot really imagine very well.

I believe that rather than through theoretical planning (whether on an individual or societal level), we can liberate ourselves by learning the principles of freedom, self-direction, self-development, and sharing, and applying them to everyday life. With each person who does so, all of humanity moves one tiny step closer to anarchy—which emerges from spontaneous order through the mutually voluntary interactions of countless people possessing information dispersed all around us; I don't think it can be instituted according to a pre-written script. I fear, however, that even some libertarians occasionally tend to forget the human brain's inability to comprehend and grasp the unimaginable complexity of our society when it comes to something they truly care about: they try to predict the unpredictable and plan the unplannable. I have no wish to repeat this mistake (so typical of socialists); I accept my role as one person among billions of others, before whom I neither abase myself nor exalt myself above them. I long for freedom, I learn how to attain it, and I share with others what I've learned (through this book, for instance); whoever wants to can join me as an equal. I strive to liberate myself, not others—and yet I simultaneously consider this very path the most effective way to liberate society as a whole, though only as long as that does not become my goal.

In the *Democracy* chapter we examined the ineffectiveness of voting in elections as a tool for bringing about (virtually any) change from an individual's standpoint; and in the *Politics* chapter, the ineffectiveness of winning and wielding mandates of public (state) power to achieve freedom. The insights from subsequent chapters, however, allow us to generalize further: both casting votes and running for them typically mean focusing on other people's lives and opinions rather than one's own—and anything like that always poses at least a threat to freedom, if not its outright erosion. Freedom is not given, freedom is taken; it comes from within ourselves—we cannot receive it as a gift from a politician or an institution. Of course, that doesn't mean a bad law restricting us will never be repealed (I'm glad when that occasionally happens); only that purposefully pursuing such a thing is an undertaking so uncertain and demanding that the energy it requires can almost always be spent more fruitfully—and above all with a far lower risk of being corrupted by power (for politicians) or buying into the illusion that I'm changing something and acting "for the good of society" when I drop slips of paper into a ballot box and argue about it with acquaintances (for voters).

In my view, the strength of the anarchoagorist path lies, among other things, in uniting external and internal freedom. Whereas the former means respect for property rights (and thus concerns interpersonal relationships and interactions), the essence of the latter lies in managing fear, cultivating conscious responsibility, and freeing oneself from various inner demons (which we achieve through self-knowledge and self-development). These two freedoms are closely intertwined, however: an environment where property rights are respected (including, above all, self-ownership) produces more responsible individuals who better understand that they are the creators of their own lives. Yet the reverse holds as well—the healthier a person's self-confidence and the fewer unprocessed (even unconscious) fears they carry, the easier it is for them to respect others and refrain from trying to restrict their property rights "for their own good" (or at least in exchange for the illusion of safety). Libertarians focus heavily on external freedom (which I consider important), yet in my opinion they unfortunately often neglect internal freedom: it bothers them when others initiate violence against them (typically through the state), they condemn such behavior (or even its perpetrators), and there they frequently stop. If we desire a society that does not intrude into our lives and property, we must first rid ourselves of fear and obedience; while each of us can only do that for ourselves, we can still inspire others to do the same (especially when not trying to).

What I consider one of the most pertinent objections to anarchoagorism focuses on how it will unfold in the future, which is why I want to address it in this chapter. Even among libertarians, one sometimes hears that anarchoagorism's effectiveness depends on only a handful of people practicing it, whereas if there were more of them, the state would begin taking repressive countermeasures against them; some even discourage me from public displays of disobedience (to laws) out of fear of sweeping reactions from public authorities. I agree that something like that could indeed happen (though not necessarily); yet hardly any path to freedom is without risk—and I don't want to abandon this one primarily because it actually works. Should the state ultimately take retaliatory steps, however, it will at least give more people a chance to see its true (violent) nature. Many people come to ideas of freedom—or outright anarchism—precisely in response to excessive or absurd regulations, as was clearly visible during the COVID pandemic, which noticeably shook citizens' faith in institutions. For completeness, I should add that my goal is certainly not to provoke anyone and I do not seek conflict with state power (nor, I believe, do most anarchoagorists); I am simply noting that if it nonetheless occurs, a side effect may be eroding the trust of (even a small) part of the public in the state's benevolence and nudging humanity (at least slightly) closer to disobedience as a social norm.

We could speculate endlessly about possible future scenarios and the risks tied to them, and still never manage to describe them all—after all, even the current state of the world in this very moment surpasses human imagination in its complexity, let alone anyone successfully planning society's development years (or decades) ahead. What can we do about that? Nothing. Let's stop striving for the impossible, and learn to live here and now—as freely as we can.

name: 22. Love
text:
I want to dedicate the final chapter to something connected not merely with anarchoagorism, but with practically everything we do in life—namely, love. We can carry out any activity from a wide variety of motives and experience all sorts of emotions while doing so. As I grow older, I understand ever more deeply that motives matter and why—even if it may not be obvious at first glance: the results of our actions primarily shape the external world, whereas our intentions primarily shape the internal one, thereby molding who we become. If I write a book or another text for the sheer joy of writing and out of a desire to share my knowledge with people, it does something utterly different to me than if I write something, say, to smear someone. The more of my life energy and time I devote to creating beautiful things, the kinder and happier a person I become; if, conversely, I choose to nurse resentment and fight (even for a good cause), I risk growing bitter over time. Two people can perform a seemingly identical activity differing solely in their inner motives; even if no one else notices the difference, it leaves its imprint inside them. By this I certainly don't mean we must never make a misstep—quite the opposite, mistakes are part of being human and move us forward; I'm only saying that everything we do, and above all why we do it, accumulates within us and shapes us.

I love freedom; I need to perceive it, to feel it—for me it is both means and end, source of strength and reward. I explore and study it, deepening and strengthening my ability not to confuse it with recklessness and arbitrariness; I'm learning to see and accept its darker sides too—to respect people who use it in ways I may find uncomfortable or even frightening. Yet as much as I've been a lover and explorer of freedom perhaps all my life, sometimes I can't resist anger and start fighting someone for it or over it—and it is in those very moments that I drift farthest away from it. Here I want to stress that I am not trying to convert the reader to (anarcho)pacifism (much as I admire its purity, I don't consider it universally viable today or in any foreseeable future); I recognize an autonomous individual's need for self-defense, yet at the same time warn against the danger of a gradual, unexpected, unnoticed, and unwanted transformation of their inner world. I see a chasm between determination to preserve one's freedom while trying to cause as little harm as possible to oneself or one's surroundings (which includes thinking about how to prevent conflict) and reveling in humiliating and shaming anyone we regard as an enemy. The desire to live one's life one's own way is different from the urge to win and defeat "the bad guys"; yet under the sway of fear, one motive can quietly swap places with the other inside us without our even realizing it.

How do we uncover something like that within ourselves? I'm afraid not even the sharpest mind can answer that question, for the higher the intelligence we possess, the more intricate ways we can invent to deceive ourselves. If we want to know the truth, we have to look inward and try to sense honestly how we truly feel. Rushing can harm the whole process (psychedelics, by contrast, can help, though I certainly do not recommend using them without thorough preparation), and moreover it will rarely be a one-off process. What emotions predominate in us regarding what we do? If fear, anger, hatred, or a desire for revenge or punishment prevails over the long haul, we are probably moving away from freedom—even in extreme cases: a soldier might enlist for the front to defend his (free) country from conquerors, for example, yet the more he hates them, the more willing he will become to sacrifice his own freedom or that of others in order to defeat them (which doesn't mean he wouldn't ultimately pay a subjectively higher price for surrender—yet that changes nothing about what I just said).

When we step away from extreme situations and return to everyday Czech life today, these principles hold even more clearly in my opinion. Angry warriors (not from the front lines, but from the warmth of their living rooms) often clamor for state solutions at the expense of individual autonomy in the name of a "higher good" (whether it concerns the migration crisis, COVID, the war in Ukraine, or Gaza—largely regardless of which side of a given conflict or issue they root for). Those, by contrast, who focus on their own lives and on finding happiness in what fulfills them—without needing to change, fix, punish, or triumph over anyone—typically do not have such strong urges to disrespect others' freedom; after all, anyone who finds meaning in what they devote themselves to (work, hobbies, relationships...) logically wants to spend their time doing just that, rather than trying to control other people.

I try to do things with love; it truly matters to me. When I fail at that in some activity, I look for ways to do it differently; if nothing changes, I take it as a signal to move on to something else. Life is too short to spend on things that don't fulfill me. I'm not at 100 percent (yet)—I still can't manage to pay fines or sign tax returns with love, and I don't know how to avoid them every single time (though I manage to avoid fines more and more often, and at least someone else fills out my tax returns for me); still, I spend the vast majority of my time (in fact, nearly all of it) on activities that give me meaning. It wasn't always this way—I've been aiming for it since childhood—and it required thinking deeply about life, changing or ending certain relationships, and acquiring the knowledge and skills to make a living from my hobbies (programming, teaching, anarchism, and self-development). During my university years I supported myself with all sorts of (mostly manual) jobs that I didn't enjoy, yet my goal was to use my free time to learn everything needed to leave them behind. If ever in the future I stop finding fulfillment in exploring the field of freedom (hard as it is to imagine), I'd rather go do something else than carry on without love and grow bitter over time. Unfortunately, I know more than a few libertarians who speak about freedom with deep resentment toward people they view as enemies of themselves or their mission. Over time, the former joy and beauty fade from the speech (and likely the inner experience) of such individuals as they focus ever more on fighting and enmity.

If I perform any activity with inner anger, I develop an aversion to it; while I may push through that (perhaps because I've made an internal commitment or identify with the cause), it isn't realistically possible for it to leave the results—and myself—untouched over time. In the *Politics* chapter, we looked at the harmful impact electoral defeats have on libertarians trying to advance freedom through democratic means: the frustration of losing causes a drift away from original values and ideals. Yet the same thing can happen to any of us, even if within political parties it poses a far more acute threat. Hateful comments on social media, condemnation, public indifference toward a long-prepared event, or (repeated) failure in trying to get an idea across can likewise breed disillusionment and bitterness in anyone; as people spreading ideas of freedom, we encounter all of that daily and have to cope with it. A prolonged inability to handle these hardships typically leads to (inner and outer) conflict, embitterment, a thirst for revenge (on anyone, sometimes the whole world), and generally into the victim role. Originally beautiful ideas insidiously turn into spiteful outbursts without their proponent even noticing—who may thus gradually, unwittingly begin doing a disservice to what they once loved so dearly. What can we do about that?

For me personally, love itself has proven to be the best feedback from reality: if it fills me while I create—if I feel it during my lectures, while writing, debating, or filming videos—it confirms the direction I'm heading. When, on the other hand, I go through a period in which I drift away from it more often (which typically begins to show during sharper exchanges in the comments, for example), I treat it as a signal that I need to change something, which usually helps; if, however, I ever stopped loving my work as a whole, I would go do something else. By the word "love," I mean that feeling of pure happiness, inner bliss, and joy that is swelling inside me even now as I write these lines; in a way, I'll certainly feel a little sad when I finish this book. Conversely, I would not use the word for tense emotions, impatience, or the urge to snap at a debate opponent for being an idiot when they can't grasp the basics of propositional logic—nor even for the potential gratification of a "won" debate if, in the end, there was no genuine understanding and mutual enrichment (but perhaps only one side's inability to keep defending its position). In the moment, such a "win" may bring satisfaction, applause, and complimentary comments, or even enrich someone in the audience, which can feel like confirmation of a job well done; yet I believe that with love and respect for our counterparts we can achieve better results for freedom (to say nothing of the effects on ourselves described above). In short, love helps me orient myself; it is my working compass on life's journey.

In early childhood, even before I learned to read, I was deeply struck by the sentence: "Love your enemies." (Matt 5:44) It stayed on my mind, and for about half my life I viewed it as an altruistic call meant to help those enemies; over time, however, I began to grasp its further implications—namely, that both my love and my hatred affect me even more powerfully than they affect others, so I get to choose what I want to live in and what my inner world will be like. Not to mention that the more people around me suffer, the worse they will treat me—especially if they dislike me. So I try to wish a happy life even to someone who hates me, because I believe that in the end it helps me too. I can't feel love for everyone all the time; yet I consider it a worthy goal (which in no way contradicts the need to defend oneself against attacks on one's integrity or autonomy).

Given the sheer volume of content I've published over the past twenty years, it doesn't surprise me that it is often interpreted in different ways and occasionally completely misinterpreted (I assume there is usually no malice behind it, just plain misunderstanding); that is why I prefer to approach important topics from multiple angles and in different forms so as to minimize misunderstandings—even if they probably cannot be avoided altogether. In the case of this book, perhaps more than anything else, I would hate for it to be read as a call to blind defiance at any cost, hatred toward state officials, or callousness; on the contrary, I ask readers to accept it as a peaceful inspiration toward an authentically free life in love.

name: Epilogue
text:
In this book, I capture my experiences with freedom, especially since completing Anarchocapitalism; most of what I have described in the preceding twenty-two chapters I learned at Ježek bez klece—my beloved school, agora, and family. Living in a democratic state turned me first into an anarcho-capitalist, which I noticed quite quickly, and then into an anarcho-agorist, which only dawned on me years later; and in truth, I still don't know exactly when it happened. For my path to anarchism, I feel deep gratitude to existence itself, to the entire universe, and to God; and it was precisely this gratitude that motivated me to write this book, through which I want to share my lived experience with others. I am putting into words something that comes to me from all around as I simply walk through this wonderful world; I would be glad if you pass it on—I claim no copyright on this book, so do with it as you please.

The message of this publication in no way refutes the principles you can read about in Anarchocapitalism; rather, I would say it complements them with further insights. I see a free, free-market, decentralized society as a suitable platform in which people can pursue happiness and live their lives in their own way; of course, this does not mean I resonate with every way they might choose to do so (I have my reservations about formal hierarchies, for example), yet I respect every individual's choice to decide even in ways that do not personally seem right to me. I consider creating parallel non-state (ideally non-hierarchical) structures—that is, agoras—to be the most effective path first and foremost to a free life for each of us, and also to a stateless order; however, I regard efforts to change society (and other people in general) as counterproductive (especially in the long run)—I believe in change that comes from within each of us.

Despite its title, Anarchoagorism does not contain only anarcho-agorist principles, though it is fully consistent with them; I add plenty of my own insights—ranging from everything concerning children and adultism, through peacefulness and my stance on revolutions, to love, self-development, an emphasis on the individual's inner world, and an aversion to trying to change others. I personally know anarcho-agorists who disagree with me on these positions; others do not consider themselves anarcho-capitalists and certainly would not identify with my first book, especially with the theses drawn from the Austrian School of economics. Pure anarcho-agorism encompasses only the decentralized creation of agoras as a means of achieving an anarchist society and the rejection of the political path toward that goal; everything beyond that foundation consists of my own convictions, which I certainly do not ascribe to other anarchists, for whom I neither can nor wish to speak.

While writing this book, I felt the need to formulate a new (as yet nonexistent) strand of anarchism; it will build on anarcho-agorism (and fully harmonize with it), while expanding it to focus on the inner world of the individual. Just as anarcho-agorism describes how anarchists can cooperate in agoras to achieve external freedom, this new anarchism would also encompass the steps a person can take within themselves to cultivate their inner freedom. I did touch on this in the Self-Development chapter (and briefly in others), though to an extent that felt insufficient to me. I expect I will need several more years to understand the things I feel and live by deeply enough to put them into words accessible even to an uninitiated reader. I would dearly love for us to meet again then—perhaps through my next book. For now, I leave you with these words: "Freedom; self-direction; self-development; sharing."

name: AMEN: aphorisms manifesting the essence of disobedience
text: I ended my book Anarchocapitalism with an analysis of many statist objections (AMEN in Czech); at the time, it seemed wisest to close my work with a polemic and refutation of counterarguments, which I do not regret, as I think it suited that book given its theoretical nature. However, I consider Anarchoagorism to be less theoretical and more practical; besides, I (hopefully) no longer feel the need to convince anyone of anything. I only wish to share ideas and inspire people who are interested; that is also why this time AMEN stands for "aphorisms manifesting the essence of disobedience." I would say that my love for aphorisms grows as I allow myself to be guided more by vivid emotions alongside consistent logic; I love when (their) poetic quality blends with compressed wisdom. On the following pages, I want to use this form to share some thoughts that are important (to me); for each saying, I will write how I perceive it and what it symbolizes to me.

chapter: AMEN: aphorisms manifesting the essence of disobedience
name: "Good people do not obey bad laws." – unknown author
text:
The subtitle of Anarchoagorism raises (quite understandable) questions for many people: Who do we consider a good person? And which laws are bad? Not only do I not know the answers, I actively do not want to know them—I would rather not divide people into good and evil; by doing so, I would (even if only in my own head) cast myself in the role of a judge qualified to decide such things, thereby placing myself above others, which is contrary to my values. Why, then, does this book bear such a subtitle? It is not about dividing people or laws into right and wrong; please let us set aside the urge to categorize for a moment and look at the meaning hidden behind it—namely, that if, instead of following current legislation, we began to live by what we ourselves are in harmony with, it would certainly bring plenty of problems, yet we would prevent far greater suffering.

When I say that good people do not obey bad laws, I am not trying to moralize; the message is meant to encourage everyone in chains to cast them off. This does not apply only to legislation (though the state typically threatens the harshest punishments); it also concerns social norms, pressures, customs, and rules, as a result of which many of us live more according to external expectations than our own inner desires. Many do not want to disappoint their parents, others crave the approval of those around them, some try at all costs to be better than everyone else, and still others fear losing their reputation... The root cause is often obedience instilled through upbringing or school, its symptom is the loss of authenticity and freedom, and its consequence is letting life slip through our fingers in pursuit of something that may seem utterly trivial on our deathbed. I love my way of being; yet I would rather risk prison, scorn, condemnation, and even a "premature" death than lose myself.

chapter: AMEN: aphorisms manifesting the essence of disobedience
name: "Anarchy is not chaos; it is spontaneous order without rulers." – Urza
text:
Most people associate the word anarchy with chaos—often with violence, disrespect, and almost always the breakdown of order. The origin of the word lies in the Greek anarchos, composed of the prefix an- (without) and the root archos (ruler); thus, anarchy does not mean the absence of rules, but of rulers. In today's heavily hierarchical society, the two blur together for many people—they cannot imagine organization without an organizer. Yet anarchists typically do not want confusion and almost never want lawlessness, which is why they most often use as their symbol a pictogram consisting of the letter A (anarchy) inside the letter O (order) to signify that they see anarchy as a (spontaneous, decentralized) arrangement of things, not chaos.

Why is the absence of rulers so often mistaken for the absence of rules? Aside from the lens mentioned above (hierarchies are so taken for granted that we struggle to imagine any other kind of order), the state convinces us from childhood that we need leaders—the media (led by public broadcasters) frame every debate, news broadcast, commentary, and program with this default assumption, while schools teach it to us not only through direct instruction, but above all through lived experience (the teacher leads the students). Almost no one challenges or debates it; for the vast majority of the population, it is an uncritically accepted given. Yet many decentralized agoras, groups, subcultures, and even companies (sometimes quite large ones) show that it can be done differently; organization does not need an organizer, and (spontaneous) order emerges from anarchy.

chapter: AMEN: aphorisms manifesting the essence of disobedience
name: "Without government, people are not lost; they are responsible." – Athena (ChatGPT)
text:
When someone rules over people and makes decisions for them, they strip them not only of freedom and autonomy, but also of responsibility; we can see this on a large scale in every state, and on a small scale in the vast majority of schools. Those who grow accustomed to obeying eventually begin to demand guidance—they feel uncomfortable without it; Stockholm syndrome gradually develops (a positive emotional and affective bond, along with dependence of the subjugated on the controller), as a result of which subjects defend their rulers and feel lost without them. This creates a feedback loop in which those lower in the hierarchy become (actually or supposedly) unable to fend for themselves without their superiors, who in turn use this as an argument for the necessity of their rule ("the average person cannot take care of themselves because they are not used to thinking independently"); it is like "solving" drug addiction by increasing the dose because the addict can no longer function without it—yet with the state, most people find this entirely reasonable (because they are addicted to it).

Without government, whether we like it or not, we become free, autonomous, and therefore responsible; the less someone else decides for us, the more we learn to decide for ourselves. This holds true for both children and adults; I get to witness this process almost every time we welcome students from conventional schools to Ježek bez klece—the freedom they gain with us is typically paralyzing for them, so for a while they do not know what to do with it. Gradually they learn, and in retrospect they often describe this process as deeply uncomfortable and exhausting; to me, these adaptations strongly resemble the process of overcoming an addiction mentioned above (because in some sense that is probably what is actually happening). From my observation, adults show similar signs when they join us from a hierarchical environment; it seems to me, however, that their withdrawal process is not as rapid as it is for children, though it takes place in them as well. While many phenomena work only within small groups, in this case I see no reason why it could not scale to much larger communities.

chapter: AMEN: aphorisms manifesting the essence of disobedience
name: "The state is a bad servant, and an evil master." – Urza
text: The subtitle of Anarchocapitalism is a variation on a well-known proverb: Fire is a good servant, but an evil master. This saying highlights the contrast between fire's usefulness as a tool for producing heat or light and its destructiveness when it spirals out of control. My analogous paraphrase reflects not only the harm and horrors inflicted by monopolies on violence around the world (both past and present), but in its first part also the conviction that—despite the efforts of many—the state cannot be kept "under control" like fire in a furnace or an internal combustion engine. Even with the best intentions of everyone involved, rulers cannot make better decisions than decentralized, autonomous individuals, because no central planner has access to the information dispersed across all of society (a thesis I analyze in detail in Anarchocapitalism); not to mention that it is impossible to ensure those best intentions, because power corrupts, and absolute power corrupts absolutely.

chapter: AMEN: aphorisms manifesting the essence of disobedience
name: "Power tends to corrupt, and absolute power corrupts absolutely." – Lord Acton
text:
The most famous remark by John Emerich Edward Dalberg-Acton (known as Lord Acton) comes from a letter addressed to Bishop Mandell Creighton. In their late nineteenth-century correspondence, these two scholars engage in a dialogue on how to judge the deeds of thirteenth- and fourteenth-century popes who orchestrated the persecution, torture, and brutal killing of many innocent people; while the cleric took a relatively conciliatory view of their actions, the baron sharply opposed his perspective. On the one hand, he argued that their conduct was no less horrific on account of the era in which they lived (a view I share as well, though I am in the minority today); above all, however, he refused to view the actions of the powerful (specifically popes and kings) in a more favorable light than those of ordinary people (which, of course, I also agree with).

Nearly a hundred and fifty years have passed since that exchange, yet unfortunately nothing at all has changed regarding the corrupting nature of power; politicians still face the very same temptations and pitfalls, and still succumb to them in the very same way. I believe the only way not to be ground down by these pressures is to strive to respect all people (without exception), to abase oneself before no one and exalt oneself above no one, and never to forget that we are all equal (not in means or abilities, but in our humanity). At the same time, I fear that participating in any (formal) hierarchy creates incentives against seeing the world this way (in involuntary hierarchies, those incentives are far stronger); we can of course resist them (and some of us manage this more easily than others), but in my view they affect everyone to some degree. Essentially all my life, I have watched people take on power with good intentions, only to end up either giving it up or being transformed by it.

chapter: AMEN: aphorisms manifesting the essence of disobedience
name: "The strength of the state is the weakness of the people." – Urza
text: What I like about this sentence is that it actually has two meanings: first, it tells us that a strong state weakens "its" citizens (making them dependent on it); at the same time, it also expresses that the strength of the state often stems from the very weakness of the people (when they feel helpless and desperate, they turn to their rulers). Unfortunately, it follows from these theses that strengthening the state generates demand for its further expansion; combined with universal suffrage, this creates a deadly cycle in which democracy leads to socialism and centralization, though other social arrangements are not immune to similar dynamics either. The security forces of totalitarian regimes, meanwhile, trample on people so brutally that out of fear they awaken the worst in them—obedience, informing on one another, apathy, distrust, and the like; those very traits then provide the richest breeding ground for further concentration of power, its consolidation, surveillance, and repression. Hopeless as that may sound, it is never too late to start working toward change; however, we must turn our focus inward, onto ourselves, rather than trying to change others—we can lead by example and leave it up to them whether they wish to join. Cooperating with like-minded people will then make it possible to create islands of freedom (agoras) in a sea of unfreedom.

chapter: AMEN: aphorisms manifesting the essence of disobedience
name: "The master's tools will never dismantle the master's house." – Audre Lorde
text:
In 1979, Audre Lorde described herself as a Black lesbian feminist in a speech at The Second Sex Conference at New York University; she titled her address "The Master's Tools Will Never Dismantle the Master's House" (the same line appeared in the speech itself), criticizing patriarchal tendencies within the feminist movement itself. Of the master's tools, she said that they may allow us temporarily to beat him at his own game, but they will never enable us to bring about genuine change. On this point I agree with her—even when we win (often temporary) victories in certain games, in the long run we actually lose by playing them, since the only clean solution is usually simply not to play.

For me personally, this line resonates most strongly in relation to the political path taken by some anarchists; I believe that if we do not want to be ruled, it makes no sense to play along with the rulers' game or give them our attention. If I were to apply this aphorism to politics and translate it into the language of Austrian economics, I would say that for the same reasons we cannot centrally plan even something as simple as the production of toilet paper, we will not be able to shrink the state in a controlled manner and organize a transition to freedom from above—simply because it is far too complex and intricate a problem, involving countless factors we cannot foresee since we lack access to the decentralized information scattered throughout society. Trying to vote and ballot our way to anarchy strikes me as about as foolish as trying to have sex our way to virginity.

chapter: AMEN: aphorisms manifesting the essence of disobedience
name: "The end (does not) justify the means." – popular saying
text:
This popular saying (without the parentheses I added) is commonly attributed to Niccolò Machiavelli; while it is not a verbatim quote from his surviving texts, in my view it accurately summarizes his ideas—especially those in The Prince. That work fascinates me in a way: on the one hand, it can be seen as the absolute antithesis of anarchist ideas; if we call the book you are currently reading a "handbook" for achieving freedom (in the sense of relinquishing power over others and refusing to submit to their rule), then we can easily regard The Prince as a manual for accumulating and maintaining power over people at any cost. On the other hand, both books describe politics in a very similar way—as a game whose ultimate goal is gaining and consolidating dominance; although Machiavelli advises how to play it as effectively as possible while my starting point is not to enter it at all, we largely agree on its rules and purpose.

I believe that the end does not justify the means—among other reasons, because the master's tools will never dismantle the master's house. If we wish to achieve virtuous ends, using malicious means corrupts not only those ends, but above all ourselves. Many people call this stance idealistic, which I wholly agree with (and see nothing wrong with); at the same time, however, I also consider it hard-headedly pragmatic—for I value myself and want to live a life that feels worthwhile not only today, but tomorrow and at its very end. I recognize that everything has a price, and that I bear the consequences of every decision not only in the external world, but within myself as well; every action I take leaves an imprint on both my conscious and subconscious mind. I am my own instrument for achieving my goals, and every means I use I will carry inside me forever. Once I start making compromises, it becomes easier to slip into further ones—until it no longer even feels strange; I would therefore rather give up realizing certain (even virtuous) intentions than pay for them with my soul.

chapter: AMEN: aphorisms manifesting the essence of disobedience
name: "Agora. Anarchy. Action!" – SEK3 / "Freedom; self-direction; self-development; sharing." – Urza
text:
Samuel Edward Konkin III used the rallying cry "Agora. Anarchy. Action!" in his New Libertarian Manifesto; personally, I regard it as the distilled message of his work. In it, he uses the word agora to refer to individual anarchist cells (much as I do in this book); at the same time, he also uses it (in the singular) to describe the ultimate state of all humanity (as the antithesis of a state-dominated population)—speaking of the path from statism to the agora. With the term anarchy, he characterizes a (stateless) condition of society; he challenges anyone who wishes to bind another person to first prove that the person committed aggression, as otherwise they have no right to do so. The third point of his slogan is action; this is how he describes the strategy for liberation—economic resistance in the gray and black markets, building parallel structures, that is, institutions that gradually replace the state until its eventual collapse.

Unfortunately, my four words do not translate quite as elegantly into other languages; yet they express my understanding of anarcho-agorism. Freedom is a state of being (inner freedom of soul and mind, outer freedom of the world), an ideal, an end, and a means; it requires care, understanding, attention, and love to flourish, and anarcho-agorism can be seen as a practical path toward it. Self-direction embodies the natural expression of a free individual; in particular, I use it to refer to self-directed education, which we deny especially to children—something that, in my opinion, represents the greatest obstacle to achieving a free society. Self-development gives us the tools to be ourselves and live our lives our own way—in other words, for disobedience, which I consider a necessary individual prerequisite for active participation in agoras. By sharing (of both material and immaterial goods, including information), I mean of course practical participation in parallel structures, as well as any free market; it is cooperation—the strength of the human species, a means to (not only material) prosperity and to freedom.

chapter: AMEN: aphorisms manifesting the essence of disobedience
name: "Freedom is not given; freedom is taken." – unknown author
text: Many people interpret this sentence as a warning of unfreedom, in the sense that someone will take our freedom away; to me, however, this aphorism has always spoken a little differently—it tells me that I cannot receive freedom from anyone else, so if I want it, I must take it myself. It is certainly conceivable that I might persuade someone to stop infringing on my autonomy; yet even then, they would not be "giving" it to me, since it never belonged to them. In the case of inner freedom, it is clearly a matter solely of my personal work with my own fear—and no one else can do that work for me. Freedom originates within ourselves; I consider it crucial to realize that unless we give it ongoing attention and care (both within ourselves and around us), we will probably lose it sooner or later—and this can happen so gradually that we might not even notice. For example, many people reacted (at least verbally) to the sudden spike in state repression during COVID; yet most of them remained indifferent to all other oppression simply because they had grown accustomed to it gradually.

chapter: AMEN: aphorisms manifesting the essence of disobedience
name: "One's freedom ends where one's fear begins." – unknown author from the Free Port community
text:
John Stuart Mill once wrote: "One's freedom ends where another's begins." I am not very fond of this quote; while it is literally true at all times, it tells us nothing useful about where any boundary actually lies—even the freedom of the brutally oppressed ends right where the freedom of their tyrants begins. Small wonder that opposing sides in countless debates routinely invoke this slogan—supporters and opponents of free speech, the war on drugs, gun control, pandemic mandates, and the like; with that sentence, you can defend virtually any position. Some time ago, the variation above appeared in one of the Free Port discussion channels (unfortunately, I do not remember the author, though perhaps they will recognize themselves when reading these lines); it presumably refers to my concept of inner freedom as the absence or mastery of fear.

What I like most about this paraphrase is its focus on finding and resolving problems within ourselves; if we want to cast off our shackles, we need to start with the ones we have placed on ourselves. Although it is only others who deprive us of external freedom—which at first glance seems unrelated to our fear—the response to external oppression often lies in working on our inner freedom; at the very least, in my view, that is an indispensable first step. The more afraid we are, the more likely any struggle we wage for external freedom will end in failure (if it even begins at all)—recall the Revolution chapter, where I describe the various traps lying in wait for all hot-headed freedom fighters. With these words I am certainly not calling for passivity—quite the opposite—I am only warning against overly militant solutions in the outside world that stem from unprocessed fears. Working through those fears typically opens up more peaceful paths for us; these often consist in steady, painstaking everyday work rather than grand gestures, so they may seem unglamorous and slow, yet they actually work.

chapter: AMEN: aphorisms manifesting the essence of disobedience
name: "Thanking someone for your own freedom is a sure way to lose it." – Urza
text:
This message, in my opinion, is closely related to the previous one; it warns against an overly passive or submissive attitude toward (potential) authorities. As an anarchist, I am often reproached for not being grateful enough for the degree of freedom I enjoy thanks to democracy; people tell me I ought to thank the current regime for allowing me to publicly proclaim anarchist ideas without risk of persecution (which is not entirely true, though compared to most of the world today—or to Czechia just half a century ago—I can speak out almost without restriction). In reality, I feel tremendous gratitude—there are countless people thanks to whom I am able to do what I do, from the authors who inspired me, through all the creators, manufacturers, suppliers, and operators of technologies such as the internet or book printing, all the way to you, my dear readers and listeners; however, I refuse to thank democratic politicians for graciously refraining from curtailing my freedom.

I am grateful to everyone who helps me (for free or for payment) or from whom I receive something (even just attention); yet I have no intention of praising anyone merely for not oppressing me. Why? Because if I did, I would be placing myself in a subordinate position to them. Many people relate to the state this way their entire lives, so it seems normal to them. If you are among them, try imagining an analogous situation in which someone advises a victim of domestic violence to be grateful to her abuser for not beating her (too) badly (and perhaps even points out that all her previous partners beat her worse). Where is that likely to lead? Naturally, to deeper oppression; whenever anyone thanks someone (even if only silently) for not hurting them, they accept oppression as the norm. People who accept this and grow accustomed to their own subjugation gradually become blind to it; that is why supporters of democracy see nothing strange in expressing gratitude to the state for refraining from aggression—just as many victims of abuse see nothing strange in doing so toward their abusers.

chapter: AMEN: aphorisms manifesting the essence of disobedience
name: "Be the change you wish to see in the world." – Mahatma Gandhi / "Freedom cannot be imposed; freedom must be lived." – Urza / "We change society by sharing, not leading." – Athena (ChatGPT)
text: All of these aphorisms highlight the absurdity of anyone (a politician, for instance, or anyone else) planning or organizing freedom for anyone other than themselves; if we want a freer world, let us live freer lives. If it proves worthwhile, others will gladly draw inspiration from us once they see the results; the more of ourselves we share with others, the better chance we give them to find something to latch onto and follow (if they themselves wish to). Yet I consider it absolutely essential to leave the decision up to each person and never force anyone into anything; besides, forcing it wouldn't work anyway—we need to grow into freedom (within ourselves). This does not apply only to political or other coercion by force; even non-violent forms of pressure tend to produce the opposite effect in the long run—attempts to persuade someone of something often provoke resistance. Seeing the solution to one's own lack of freedom (or other problems) in what others should or should not do corresponds to a victim mentality; a creator, by contrast, understands that they hold their life in their own hands (which is also the attitude far more likely to inspire others).

chapter: AMEN: aphorisms manifesting the essence of disobedience
name: "The spirit of the game stands above the letter of the rules." – Gary Gygax
text:
Gary Gygax was one of the two creators of the original 1974 edition of the legendary game Dungeons & Dragons; it sparked the rise of the entire tabletop RPG genre and served as the template for many titles, including the Czech game Dračí doupě ("Dragon's Lair"), which I spent a large part of my adolescence playing and which shaped me to a great extent. Nearly every player of this or any similar role-playing game understands what Gary Gygax meant by his statement: rules are a tool for our enjoyment, and we should not become slaves to following them to the letter in every situation; at any point, we can agree to set the rules aside if we find that doing so improves the overall experience. However, I believe that the quote above can also be read as a metaphor—one that, in my view, reaches far beyond the gaming world of dragons and magic.

Beyond Ježek bez klece, where I have volunteered for years, my curiosity led me to dozens of self-directed schools and similar collectives, where I studied different ways of making decisions and establishing norms. Despite expecting the decisive factor to be the approval mechanism itself (consensus-seeking, majority voting over a minority, and so on), repeated observations pointed me instead toward the crucial role of how rules—and the procedures for creating them—are codified. The more precisely everything is defined (and written down), the more often everyone's attention shifts away from the meaning and spirit of the rules toward the letter of various provisions (including hunting for loopholes and ways to exploit them); conversely, collectives with very loosely defined (often merely oral) conventions focus most on their underlying meaning and spirit. I am not claiming that writing rules down can never be helpful; I am merely pointing out that most people fail to realize how much such codification diverts attention away from human needs and onto the rules themselves.

chapter: AMEN: aphorisms manifesting the essence of disobedience
name: "Love your enemies." – Jesus (Matthew 5:44)
text:
Quotes from Jesus are rarely received warmly in atheistic Czechia; in anarchist circles this holds doubly true, since for nearly two thousand years all manner of authoritarians have abused his teachings to gain, maintain, and enforce power over their fellow human beings. For me, however, Jesus represents (among other things) a functional archetype of the loving and compassionate human being I aspire to become; even if I were ever to discover with absolute certainty that he never existed, it would change nothing about my effort to move closer to him (as an ideal). I enjoy reading the Bible; the older I get, the more passages speak to me—resonating with my growing life experience. I have no illusions that I will ever be able to fully understand it; yet it continues to enrich me, and in my view it also complements the Buddhist teachings I practice as well. This approach often provokes displeasure among Christians and condescension among Buddhists, while atheists think I have lost my mind; yet to me, this path makes complete sense.

I know no one capable of constant, unconditional love for all people (including those "enemies"); nevertheless, I regard it as one of my life ideals. Why do I want to love every person regardless of what they do or who they are? Not primarily for others' sake, but above all for my own; the outer world can be ennobled by love, whereas the inner world can be completely transformed by it. Of course, loving everyone does not mean agreeing with everyone, let alone supporting their actions; nor does it imply that we cannot stand up to them or defend ourselves against them. Love, however, protects us from losing our way in the face of severe trials and trading our original (perhaps noble) direction for vengeance or delight in another's suffering; many people do not even notice such a shift happening, because they are too busy fighting and blinded by "righteous anger." Intellect will not help us much against these traps, because the sharper our mind, the more cleverly it can deceive us; there is immense strength in humility, compassion, and respect for every human being.

chapter: AMEN: aphorisms manifesting the essence of disobedience
name: "If we cannot leave people their freedom, how can we entrust them with power?" – unknown author
text: I often hear the claim that humanity is not (yet) ready for anarchy; supposedly, once we become more responsible and less indifferent, we might be able to govern ourselves, but not until then. Personally, I see it the exact opposite way—the more "corrupt" a population is, the greater the danger posed by the concentration of power. Critics of anarchism—who often seek an illusion of safety in statism—unfortunately forget that a government is generally drawn from the very society it is meant to rule, and is therefore burdened with the same vices; moreover, those vices are typically amplified, since the opportunity to control the state apparatus tends to attract domineering and unscrupulous individuals. Freedom can be understood as a person's power over themselves; if we start from the premise that people are not (yet) capable of bearing even that, it surely makes no sense to entrust them with power not only over their own lives, but over the lives of others as well (not even indirectly through the power to elect representatives for such a role—someone unfit to handle their own freedom can hardly decide competently who would make a good leader for themselves and everyone else).

chapter: AMEN: aphorisms manifesting the essence of disobedience
name: "Pain is inevitable, suffering is optional." – Buddha
text: For many years, I understood this part of the Buddha's teaching only on a theoretical level; I owe my practical grasp of it (and I genuinely feel that gratitude) to a paragliding accident I survived with twenty-five broken bones and internal injuries. After a few days in a hospital bed, it occurred to me to put this wisdom to the test; the hospital staff granted my request to discontinue the morphine so that I could have the chance to better understand what the Buddha meant. I came to understand that we have the ability to perceive pain as nothing more than a signal from the body; what we do with that signal depends solely on us—we can suffer, or we can choose not to—it is a choice (though not always a conscious one). I am not speaking of "overcoming" pain through sheer willpower (which I consider counterproductive in this context), but of simply accepting it; not everyone is always capable of this (even I cannot do it at all times or with any level of pain), yet it is something that can be practiced. How does this insight relate to anarchism? I regard it as crucial for working with inner freedom and fear; once we learn to accept pain, our tendency to succumb to fear (and thus slip into a victim mindset) drops dramatically.

chapter: AMEN: aphorisms manifesting the essence of disobedience
name: "We cause our own psychological pain." – Marshall Rosenberg / "We cause our own pain." – Gabriela Ježková
text:
Marshall Rosenberg's Nonviolent Communication changed my life (though I cannot claim any great mastery of it—I am still learning); with its help, this peacemaker managed to reconcile not only feuding families and workplaces, but also criminals with their victims, and even warring tribes that had been murdering each other for generations. He built his skills on an understanding of basic principles of the human psyche—among them the insight that we cause our own psychological pain. It is a reaction to the outside world—what hurts us is not its state as such (which is neither objectively good nor bad; it simply is), but our interpretation of it; different people evaluate the very same situation differently—it hurts some and leaves others unharmed (depending on the state of their inner world). There is nothing that wounds everyone psychologically; precisely because (unlike physical injury) what hurts us is our own reaction to a stimulus, not the stimulus itself.

The vast majority of people tend to dispute this thesis, so I have spent dozens upon dozens of hours defending it; all the more surprising was Gabriela's reaction, when she not only did not dispute it, but countered: "And why only psychological? I would say we cause all of our pain ourselves." In other words, she was probably pointing to the same thing the Buddha meant regarding suffering. Psychological wounds arise from our reaction to the outside world; physical injuries do occur directly, yet once we learn how, we can work freely with the pain associated with them (their other consequences, of course, can still be severe or even fatal). I consider working with pain an important (and likely essential) step toward overcoming the fear of it (and thus toward disobedience); taking responsibility for one's own suffering is the surest path not only to minimizing it, but above all to freedom.

chapter: AMEN: aphorisms manifesting the essence of disobedience
name: "Everything you lose through your own authenticity is an illusion anyway." – unknown author
text: This is my translation of the English saying: "Anything you lose by being real is fake." In my view, this aphorism holds a deep truth about authenticity. The more clearly we say #no_to_obedience and live our lives on our own terms (rather than according to other people's expectations), the more we risk rejection, social condemnation, loss of reputation, and alienation from the people around us. Hard as it may be to deal with those consequences, we have not lost anything wholly real—by showing the truth, we cannot lose anything that was not at least partly built on an illusion; if someone turns away from us upon discovering who we truly are, for example, they never truly wanted to be with us in the first place. If we accept the pain that comes from such losses and do not resist them, the environment around us will begin to mirror our authenticity; and that will show in our relationships, projects, work, and hobbies—we can free ourselves on every front.

chapter: AMEN: aphorisms manifesting the essence of disobedience
name: "The criterion of truth is that it works, even if nobody is prepared to acknowledge it." – Ludwig von Mises / "Truth prevails." – Jan Hus
text:
The Austrian economist Ludwig Heinrich Edler von Mises viewed truth (and not only truth) very pragmatically; he believed it ultimately prevails simply because it yields better results than falsehood—regardless of whether society or individuals accept or reject it. In the context of his work, he was speaking primarily of economic laws; yet the validity of this statement extends far beyond them, as he was well aware. The more accurate (and therefore truer) our model of reality is for describing the world around us, the better we are able to achieve our goals; this means that true propositions enjoy a fundamental "evolutionary" advantage over false ones. It follows that sharing information more often leads to the triumph of truth than of falsehood; and if freedom is truly good for people (which I firmly believe), it also leads toward achieving freedom (which is indeed slowly happening over the long run).

The Czech presidential standard bears the motto "TRUTH PREVAILS," originally attributed to Jan Hus, popularized by Tomáš Garrigue Masaryk, and expanded by Václav Havel into the sentence: "Truth and love must prevail over lies and hatred." Given that I consider this motto profoundly true, I find it amusingly paradoxical that Czech presidents invoke it and display it on a state symbol; for I believe that the triumph of truth (and love) will inevitably bring about the end of state oppression as well. The power of the state rests on deeply ingrained statism; the vast majority of us are indoctrinated into it by the current educational system, which relies on manipulation (typically through punishments and rewards)—something directly at odds with any genuine commitment to truth.

chapter: AMEN: aphorisms manifesting the essence of disobedience
name: "ACAB" – a (not only) anarchist saying
text: ACAB is an acronym for "All Cops Are Bastards" (in Czech, "všichni policajti jsou parchanti"). Of course, I do not think that every member of the police force is necessarily an unscrupulous scoundrel; undoubtedly there are individuals among them who have no desire to deliberately harm anyone (perhaps they simply could not find better work on the labor market), or who even genuinely view their job as a way to help the weak and protect the defenseless. Yet it is important (regardless of whatever personal qualities they may have) not to forget that they remain agents of the largest legalized mafia. I am certainly not encouraging hatred toward individual police officers (they are human too); however, I do warn against the danger of interacting with them—they can sometimes be polite and pleasant, yet they remain public officials, meaning that anything we say to them they are permitted (and often legally required) to use against us, our loved ones, or anyone else (and of course they are allowed to lie about it—which they routinely do). I examine exactly what to watch out for in my lecture "Anarchocapitalism: How (Not) to Talk to Police (and Others)" ("Anarchokapitalismus: Jak (ne)mluvit (nejen) s policajty?"); a recording is freely available online on the Free Port channel (Kanál Svobodného přístavu).

chapter: AMEN: aphorisms manifesting the essence of disobedience
name: "Life has more imagination than we carry in our dreams." – Christopher Columbus
text: One of my favorite quotes is commonly attributed to the skilled navigator and ruthless colonizer Christopher Columbus. Much as I disagree with many of his actions and his overall attitude toward people, I find myself living this statement constantly; it has resonated with me ever since I first came across it, nearly thirty years ago. It recently occurred to me that replacing the word "life" with "the free market" yields a libertarian aphorism illustrating how astonishing outcomes of human action can never be achieved through human design (as Friedrich August von Hayek put it: "the result of human action, but not of human design"). Above all, however, this quote speaks to me as a reminder to stay open to everything, avoid dogmatism, and humbly embrace all the wondrous beauty of the world; I have no idea what tomorrow will bring, yet today something is real to me that only yesterday was an unattainable fantasy.
